questions.title: Access to exactly one bucket
questions.summary: IAM can bind directly on individual resources such as buckets — the only scope that exposes one bucket without the project.
questions.question: Quillon Press shares print-ready proofs with an outside typesetting agency. The agency's editor, who has a Google account, must read every object in the proofs-2026 Cloud Storage bucket and nothing else in the publishing project. The bucket uses uniform bucket-level access, and new proofs arrive daily. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the partner Storage Object Viewer on the project.
options.B: Grant the partner Storage Object Viewer on the bucket.
options.C: Add the partner to the bucket's access control list with read access.
options.D: Generate a signed URL for each object and send the URLs to the partner.

explanation.summary: IAM roles can be granted on an individual bucket, so the partner can read that bucket's objects without any access to the rest of the project.

option_breakdown.A: A project grant is inherited by every bucket in the project, which exposes more than one bucket.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A bucket-level grant of Storage Object Viewer covers that bucket's objects and nothing else.
option_breakdown.C: Uniform bucket-level access disables ACLs, so access is granted with IAM only.
option_breakdown.D: Signed URLs cover single objects, expire, and miss objects added later; they are not standing access to a bucket.

questions.title: No predefined role matches exactly
questions.summary: When no predefined role matches, a custom role with exactly those permissions is least privilege.
questions.question: A role must allow listing and getting Compute Engine instances and nothing else. You review the predefined roles and none matches that set without carrying extra permissions. What should you do?

options.A: Grant an existing predefined role.
options.B: Create a custom role containing exactly the required permissions.
options.C: Grant a basic role such as Owner, Editor or Viewer.
options.D: Add an IAM condition to the role binding.

explanation.summary: When no predefined role matches, a custom role with exactly the listed permissions is the least-privilege answer.

option_breakdown.A: Predefined roles are curated per-service permission sets; when none matches the required permissions, the nearest one over-grants.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. When no predefined role matches, a custom role with exactly the listed permissions is the least-privilege answer.
option_breakdown.C: Basic roles are coarse legacy roles spanning every service in a project and should not be used where least privilege matters.
option_breakdown.D: IAM conditions restrict when or on which resources a binding applies; they narrow an existing grant rather than defining a new permission set.

questions.title: Access expiring at quarter end
questions.summary: IAM conditions express expiry and resource-name predicates on the binding itself.
questions.question: A contractor at Ashgrove Studios needs to read objects only in buckets whose names begin with shared-, and only until the quarter ends on 31 March. Afterwards the access must lapse with nobody having to remember to remove it. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the Viewer basic role on the project until 31 March.
options.B: Create an IAM deny policy that blocks other buckets after 31 March.
options.C: Grant Storage Object Viewer with an IAM condition on the bucket-name prefix and an expiry time.
options.D: Grant Storage Object Viewer on the project and remove it on 31 March.

explanation.summary: IAM conditions express both the expiry date and a resource-name predicate on the binding itself, which no static role can do.

option_breakdown.A: Basic roles can't carry IAM conditions, so there is no 'until 31 March', and Viewer spans every service and bucket in the project.
option_breakdown.B: A deny policy only removes permissions; it grants nothing, so the contractor would still have no access to the shared- buckets.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. IAM conditions express both the expiry date and a resource-name predicate on the binding itself, which no static role can do.
option_breakdown.D: Unconditional Storage Object Viewer covers every bucket in the project, and removing it depends on someone remembering to.

questions.title: Even Owners must not delete these buckets
questions.summary: Deny policies evaluate before allow policies and cannot be overridden by any role.
questions.question: Principals who hold Owner must nonetheless be prevented from deleting a specific set of production buckets, and the control must not be defeatable by granting more roles. What should you do?

options.A: Grant those principals a custom role without storage.buckets.delete.
options.B: Add an IAM condition to their Owner binding that excludes the buckets.
options.C: Alert on audit log entries that delete the buckets.
options.D: Create an IAM deny policy.

explanation.summary: Deny policies are evaluated before allow policies and cannot be overridden by any role grant, including Owner.

option_breakdown.A: A new role adds permissions; they keep Owner, which still allows deletion.
option_breakdown.B: IAM conditions can't be used with basic roles such as Owner.
option_breakdown.C: An alert reports the deletion after it has happened.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Deny policies are evaluated before allow policies, so no role grant, Owner included, can override them.

questions.title: Google already ships the right role
questions.summary: roles/pubsub.publisher matches exactly; a custom role would duplicate it and need maintenance.
questions.question: A team needs to publish messages to Pub/Sub topics and do nothing else. Google already ships a role for precisely this. What should you do?

options.A: Grant an existing predefined role.
options.B: Add an IAM condition to the role binding.
options.C: Create an IAM deny policy.
options.D: Create a custom role containing exactly the required permissions.

explanation.summary: roles/pubsub.publisher is the predefined role for exactly this permission set; creating a custom role would duplicate it and require ongoing maintenance.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. roles/pubsub.publisher is the predefined role for exactly this permission set; creating a custom role would duplicate it and require ongoing maintenance.
option_breakdown.B: A condition limits when or where a role applies; the team still needs a role that grants publishing.
option_breakdown.C: A deny policy blocks permissions; it can't grant the ability to publish.
option_breakdown.D: Custom roles must be maintained by hand as services add permissions; they are unnecessary when a predefined role already fits.

questions.title: Everyone holds Editor in production
questions.summary: Basic roles span every service; replace Editor with the predefined roles each principal actually needs, using role recommendations as evidence.
questions.question: An audit finds that all developers hold the basic Editor role on the production project, although most of them only deploy Cloud Run services and read logs. You must remediate the finding following least privilege. What should you do first?

options.A: Keep Editor and add an IAM condition that limits it to business hours.
options.B: Use IAM role recommendations to replace Editor with the predefined roles each developer uses.
options.C: Replace Editor with Owner on a smaller group of senior developers and route changes through them.
options.D: Leave Editor in place and create a deny policy that blocks every permission developers do not use.

explanation.summary: Editor grants write access to almost every service in the project, which is why audits flag it. The remediation is to find out what each principal really uses — role recommendations from Active Assist are built for exactly this — and bind narrowly scoped predefined roles such as Cloud Run Developer and Logs Viewer instead.

option_breakdown.A: A time condition limits when the over-grant applies, not what it grants.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Evidence-based replacement of a basic role with predefined roles is least privilege without breaking the developers' real work.
option_breakdown.C: Owner is broader still, and concentrating it on a few people does not fix the over-grant.
option_breakdown.D: Deny policies are guardrails for specific dangerous permissions; enumerating everything a developer does not need is unmaintainable and still leaves the basic role in place.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID --flatten='bindings[].members' \
  --filter='bindings.role=roles/editor'
gcloud recommender recommendations list --project=PROJECT_ID --location=global \
  --recommender=google.iam.policy.Recommender

questions.title: VM calls an API with no key on disk
questions.summary: An attached service account is served short-lived tokens by the metadata server.
questions.question: A Compute Engine application must call the Pub/Sub API with its own least-privilege identity, and no credential file may exist on the instance. What should you do?

options.A: Grant Service Account Token Creator so the principal can impersonate the service account.
options.B: Configure Workload Identity Federation for the external workload.
options.C: Configure Workload Identity Federation for GKE, binding the Kubernetes service account to the IAM service account.
options.D: Create a dedicated service account and attach it to the resource.

explanation.summary: A dedicated service account attached to the instance is served short-lived tokens by the metadata server, so no key ever exists on disk.

option_breakdown.A: Impersonation still needs some identity on the VM to make the request, which is the problem to solve.
option_breakdown.B: Workload Identity Federation is for workloads outside Google Cloud; a VM can have a service account attached.
option_breakdown.C: Workload Identity Federation for GKE is for Pods on GKE, not Compute Engine VMs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A dedicated service account attached to the instance is served short-lived tokens by the metadata server, so no key ever exists on disk.

questions.title: Pod reaches Cloud Storage without a secret
questions.summary: Workload Identity binds the Kubernetes SA to an IAM SA, issuing short-lived credentials.
questions.question: A Pod in GKE must access a Cloud Storage bucket using a Google Cloud identity, with no key mounted as a Kubernetes secret. What should you do?

options.A: Workload Identity Federation for GKE, for the Pod's KSA.
options.B: Configure Workload Identity Federation for the external workload.
options.C: Create a service account key and store it with the application.
options.D: Use the project's default Compute Engine service account.

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Federation for GKE binds the Kubernetes service account to an IAM service account, so Pods receive short-lived credentials with no secret to mount.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Workload Identity Federation for GKE binds the Kubernetes service account to an IAM service account, so Pods receive short-lived credentials with no secret to mount.
option_breakdown.B: Federation with an external provider is for workloads outside Google Cloud; GKE has its own built-in form.
option_breakdown.C: A key is the long-lived secret that must not be mounted.
option_breakdown.D: Pods would use the node's identity, shared by every Pod on the node and broad by default.

questions.title: External CI deploys with no keys allowed
questions.summary: Workload Identity Federation exchanges the provider's OIDC token for short-lived credentials.
questions.question: A CI pipeline running outside Google Cloud must deploy into it, and security has banned downloadable service account keys entirely. What should you configure?

options.A: Use the project's default Compute Engine service account.
options.B: Configure Workload Identity Federation for the external workload.
options.C: Create a dedicated service account and attach it to the resource.
options.D: Grant Service Account Token Creator so the principal can impersonate the service account.

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Federation exchanges the external provider's OIDC token for short-lived Google Cloud credentials, removing the need for any key.

option_breakdown.A: The default service account can only be used from outside Google Cloud with a key, which is banned.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Workload Identity Federation exchanges the external provider's OIDC token for short-lived Google Cloud credentials, removing the need for any key.
option_breakdown.C: Attaching a service account only works for resources running in Google Cloud.
option_breakdown.D: To impersonate, the pipeline must first authenticate as a Google principal, which without keys means federation anyway.

questions.title: Privileged action attributable to a person
questions.summary: Impersonation issues a short-lived token while audit logs still record the human principal.
questions.question: An engineer must occasionally run a deployment as a privileged service account, and every such action must remain attributable to them personally in the audit log. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the engineer Service Account User on the service account.
options.B: Grant the service account's privileged roles to the engineer directly.
options.C: Grant Service Account Token Creator so the principal can impersonate the service account.
options.D: Create a service account key and store it with the application.

explanation.summary: Impersonation issues a short-lived token while the audit log still records the human principal who requested it, which preserves attribution.

option_breakdown.A: Service Account User lets the engineer attach the account to resources; it doesn't let them get tokens to act as it.
option_breakdown.B: Actions are attributable, but the engineer then holds the privileges all the time instead of using the service account occasionally.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Impersonation issues a short-lived token while the audit log still records the human principal who requested it, which preserves attribution.
option_breakdown.D: A key is a long-lived credential, and actions taken with it are logged as the service account, not the engineer.

questions.title: Distinguish each app's API calls
questions.summary: A per-application attached service account makes calls individually attributable.
questions.question: Several applications share one project, and an audit requires each application's API calls to be individually distinguishable and separately authorisable. What should you do?

options.A: Create a service account key and store it with the application.
options.B: Use the project's default Compute Engine service account.
options.C: Grant Service Account Token Creator so the principal can impersonate the service account.
options.D: Create a dedicated service account and attach it to the resource.

explanation.summary: Giving each application its own attached service account is what makes its calls individually attributable and separately authorisable.

option_breakdown.A: A key is a long-lived secret, and it doesn't separate the applications unless each has its own account.
option_breakdown.B: Every application would share one identity, so their calls can't be told apart or authorised separately.
option_breakdown.C: Impersonation lets people act as an account; each application still needs its own identity.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Giving each application its own attached service account is what makes its calls individually attributable and separately authorisable.

questions.title: One-hour token with no stored secret
questions.summary: Short-lived credential generation via Token Creator yields a time-bounded access token.
questions.question: A script must obtain a token valid for about an hour to call an API as a service account, with no long-lived credential existing anywhere. What should you do?

options.A: Grant Token Creator to the script's identity and impersonate the service account.
options.B: Create a service-account key, use it, and delete it after an hour.
options.C: Store a service-account key in Secret Manager and read it at runtime.
options.D: Grant the script's identity roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on the service account.

explanation.summary: Token Creator lets the caller mint a short-lived access token for the service account (one hour by default); no key ever exists.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Token Creator lets the caller mint a short-lived access token for the service account (one hour by default); no key ever exists.
option_breakdown.B: A key is a long-lived credential for as long as it exists, and deleting it is a manual step.
option_breakdown.C: A key in Secret Manager is still a long-lived key that anything able to read the secret can copy.
option_breakdown.D: Service Account User lets you attach the account to a resource; it does not let you mint tokens.

questions.title: An inherited role that one project must not have
questions.summary: A child resource cannot remove an allow binding inherited from a parent; change the grant at its source.
questions.question: The analytics group holds BigQuery Data Viewer on a folder with twelve projects. One of those projects now holds regulated data that the group must not read. You try to remove the role in that project's IAM policy but the binding does not appear there. What should you do?

options.A: Add a binding in the project for the same role with an empty member list, which cancels the inherited one.
options.B: Remove the folder grant, and grant the eleven projects directly.
options.C: Grant the group roles/browser in the project, which overrides the inherited data role.
options.D: Wait for the next IAM propagation cycle, after which the project-level removal will be possible.

explanation.summary: Allow policies are additive down the hierarchy: a project inherits its ancestors' bindings and cannot subtract them. To exclude one project, change where the grant is made — or move the project — or, for a guardrail, use a deny policy.

option_breakdown.A: There is no such cancellation; policies only add access.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Change the grant at its source, or restructure the hierarchy.
option_breakdown.C: Roles do not override each other; Browser adds, it does not remove.
option_breakdown.D: Inherited bindings never become removable at the child.

questions.title: A Google-managed service agent needs access in another project
questions.summary: Service agents are Google-managed service accounts; when a service reads another project's resource, grant the agent.
questions.question: A Cloud Run deployment in project `app` fails to pull an image from an Artifact Registry repository in project `images`. The error names `service-APP_NUMBER@serverless-robot-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. What should you do?

options.A: Create a user-managed service account called serverless-robot-prod in project images.
options.B: Download a key for the service account named in the error and store it in Secret Manager.
options.C: Grant that service agent Artifact Registry Reader on the repository in project images.
options.D: Make the repository public.

explanation.summary: The account in the error is the Cloud Run service agent, a Google-managed service account that the platform uses to pull images. When the image lives in another project, that agent needs Artifact Registry Reader there.

option_breakdown.A: Service agents are created by Google; you cannot create one with that name, and you do not need to.
option_breakdown.B: You cannot create keys for service agents, and keys are not the problem.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Grant the Google-managed identity that performs the pull.
option_breakdown.D: Public repositories expose images to everyone to fix one missing grant.

questions.title: Deploying a service that runs as a service account
questions.summary: Attaching a service account to a resource requires iam.serviceAccounts.actAs — Service Account User on that account.
questions.question: A developer with Cloud Run Developer on a project runs `gcloud run deploy --service-account=orders-sa@...` and gets a permission error mentioning `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`. The service must run as orders-sa. What should you grant?

options.A: Service Account User on orders-sa, to the developer.
options.B: Service Account Admin on the project, to the developer.
options.C: Cloud Run Admin on the project, to orders-sa.
options.D: Service Account Token Creator on the project, to orders-sa.

explanation.summary: Deploying a resource that runs as a service account requires permission to act as that account (iam.serviceAccounts.actAs), which roles/iam.serviceAccountUser carries. Granting it on the one service account keeps it narrow.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. actAs on exactly that service account.
option_breakdown.B: Admin lets the developer create and delete service accounts, which is much more than needed.
option_breakdown.C: The error is about the developer's permission, not what orders-sa can do.
option_breakdown.D: Token Creator granted to the service account itself does not let the developer attach it.

questions.title: One Cloud Run service calling another private service
questions.summary: The calling service's attached service account gets a short-lived ID token from the metadata server.
questions.question: Cloud Run service `frontend` must call Cloud Run service `pricing`, which does not allow unauthenticated access. No keys may be stored anywhere. What should you do?

options.A: Create a key for frontend's service account and pass it in an HTTP header.
options.B: Allow unauthenticated invocations on pricing and restrict it with a VPC firewall rule.
options.C: Share an API key between the two services through an environment variable.
options.D: Grant Invoker on pricing, and send an ID token from the metadata server.

explanation.summary: The metadata server issues short-lived, audience-bound ID tokens for the service's attached identity. pricing checks the token and the Invoker binding; nothing long-lived exists.

option_breakdown.A: Keys are long-lived secrets, exactly what the requirement rules out.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Run's public endpoint is not governed by VPC firewall rules; this opens the service.
option_breakdown.C: API keys identify a project, not a caller, and are a stored secret.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Short-lived tokens from the attached identity, authorised by IAM.

questions.title: Only one repository's pipeline may use the federation
questions.summary: An attribute condition on the workload identity provider restricts which external tokens are accepted.
questions.question: A workload identity pool trusts GitHub Actions. Only workflows from the repository `acme/infra` should ever be able to exchange tokens through the provider, even if someone later grants a broader principal set access by mistake. What should you configure?

options.A: A VPC Service Controls perimeter around the project.
options.B: An attribute condition requiring repository acme/infra.
options.C: A service account key restricted to GitHub's IP ranges.
options.D: A separate workload identity pool for each workflow file.

explanation.summary: The provider's attribute condition is evaluated on every token exchange; tokens that fail it are rejected before any IAM binding is considered. Attribute mappings then let IAM bindings target that repository precisely.

option_breakdown.A: Perimeters restrict API access to resources, not which GitHub tokens the provider accepts.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Rejects tokens from any other repository at the provider itself.
option_breakdown.C: Keys are what federation exists to avoid.
option_breakdown.D: Pools per workflow add sprawl without restricting which repository's tokens are accepted.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers update-oidc github --workload-identity-pool=ci \
  --location=global --attribute-condition="assertion.repository=='acme/infra'"

questions.title: A custom role needed in forty projects
questions.summary: A custom role created in a project can be granted only in that project; create it at the organisation to reuse it.
questions.question: Security at Aldermoor Group designed a custom role for incident responders. It must be granted in forty projects across several folders of the organization, and changes to its permissions must be made in one place. Where should you create it?

options.A: In each of the forty projects, from the same YAML definition.
options.B: In one project, then grant it in the other thirty-nine projects.
options.C: In a folder, which then offers it to every project below.
options.D: At the organisation, then grant it in each project.

explanation.summary: Custom roles can be defined at the organisation or at a project. A project-level custom role can only be used in that project; an organisation-level custom role can be granted on any resource in the organisation and is updated once.

option_breakdown.A: Forty copies drift and must be updated forty times.
option_breakdown.B: A project-level custom role cannot be granted in other projects.
option_breakdown.C: Custom roles cannot be defined on folders.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. One definition, grantable anywhere in the organisation.

questions.title: Every binding that applies to a project, including inherited ones
questions.summary: gcloud projects get-ancestors-iam-policy shows the policies of the project and all its ancestors.
questions.question: During an access review, you need every IAM binding that affects one project: those set on the project itself and those inherited from its folders and the organisation. What should you retrieve, in one step?

options.A: The IAM policies of the project and all its ancestors.
options.B: The project's own IAM policy.
options.C: The organisation's IAM policy.
options.D: The description of the Owner role.

explanation.summary: get-iam-policy returns only the bindings set directly on the project. get-ancestors-iam-policy walks up the hierarchy and returns the project's policy together with those of its folders and organisation.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. gcloud projects get-ancestors-iam-policy returns the project's policy and every ancestor's in one call.
option_breakdown.B: Direct bindings only; inherited access is invisible here.
option_breakdown.C: Only the organisation's own policy, not the folders or the project.
option_breakdown.D: Describes a role's permissions, not who holds it.

questions.title: Granting a Kubernetes service account access directly
questions.summary: Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets you bind IAM roles directly to a Kubernetes service account principal.
questions.question: Pods in namespace `orders` run as Kubernetes service account `orders-ksa` on a cluster with Workload Identity Federation for GKE enabled. They need to publish to one Pub/Sub topic, and the team prefers not to create and manage an extra IAM service account. What should you do?

options.A: Mount a key for the node's service account as a Kubernetes Secret.
options.B: Grant the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the node pool's service account.
options.C: Grant Publisher on the topic to orders-ksa's principal identifier.
options.D: Annotate orders-ksa with the project's default Compute Engine service account.

explanation.summary: With Workload Identity Federation for GKE, a Kubernetes service account is an IAM principal (principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/PROJECT.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/orders/sa/orders-ksa). You can grant it roles directly; linking to an IAM service account is optional.

option_breakdown.A: Keys are exactly what Workload Identity removes.
option_breakdown.B: The node's identity is shared by every Pod on the node, which breaks least privilege.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A direct grant to the Kubernetes service account's principal.
option_breakdown.D: The default compute account is broad and shared; it is the wrong identity to borrow.

questions.title: A least-privilege identity for GKE nodes
questions.summary: Give GKE nodes a minimal custom service account instead of the Editor-bearing default compute account.
questions.question: A new GKE Standard node pool would use the Compute Engine default service account, which holds Editor in this project. Nodes only need to write logs and metrics and pull images; workloads use their own identities. What should you do?

options.A: Keep the default service account but restrict it with the cloud-platform access scope.
options.B: A dedicated node service account with only those roles.
options.C: Use a service account key for the nodes, stored as a Kubernetes Secret.
options.D: Grant Owner to the default service account so node upgrades never fail on permissions.

explanation.summary: Every Pod that can reach the metadata server could otherwise borrow the node's identity. A minimal node service account, with only the logging, monitoring and image-pull permissions nodes need, removes the Editor exposure.

option_breakdown.A: The cloud-platform scope allows everything the service account's roles allow — here, Editor.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A purpose-built, minimal identity for the nodes.
option_breakdown.C: Keys are unnecessary; nodes use their attached service account.
option_breakdown.D: Owner makes the exposure worse, not better.

questions.title: Retiring a service account you think is unused
questions.summary: Disable a service account first: it is reversible, unlike deletion, and shows whether anything still depends on it.
questions.question: A service account named legacy-batch appears unused, but nobody is sure. You want to retire it while being able to recover quickly if a forgotten job depended on it. What should you do first?

options.A: Delete it; deleted service accounts are restored automatically when something calls them.
options.B: Remove all its roles and delete its keys, leaving it enabled.
options.C: Rename it to deprecated-legacy-batch so any caller receives a clear error.
options.D: Disable it, watch for failures, and delete it later.

explanation.summary: Disabling a service account blocks its authentication immediately while preserving the account and its bindings, so re-enabling restores everything. Deletion is harder to reverse, and after the undelete window it is permanent.

option_breakdown.A: Deletion is not undone automatically; undelete is manual and time-limited.
option_breakdown.B: Stripping roles loses the bindings you would need to restore.
option_breakdown.C: Service account IDs cannot be renamed; only the display name changes.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A safe, reversible first step.

questions.title: Stop new default service accounts receiving Editor
questions.summary: The iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts constraint stops default service accounts getting Editor.
questions.question: At Westbury Labs, when a project enables the Compute Engine API, its default compute service account receives the Editor role automatically. Security wants that automatic grant to stop in every new project created anywhere in the organization. What should you do?

options.A: Enforce iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts.
options.B: Delete the default service account in every project after it is created.
options.C: Add a deny policy on the Editor role for all service accounts.
options.D: Enable Data Access audit logs so the grant is detected.

explanation.summary: This boolean constraint prevents default service accounts from receiving the Editor role automatically when they are created, so new projects start without that broad grant.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The documented guardrail for exactly this automatic grant.
option_breakdown.B: Deleting it breaks workloads that expect it and does not change the default for future projects.
option_breakdown.C: Deny policies deny permissions, not roles, and a blanket rule on Editor's permissions would break legitimate users.
option_breakdown.D: Detection after the fact does not stop the grant.

questions.title: Who is allowed to impersonate a service account
questions.summary: Access to a service account is set on the service account itself as a resource; read its own IAM policy.
questions.question: You need to find out who can impersonate the deploy-sa service account or attach it to resources. Where do you look?

options.A: The roles granted to deploy-sa in the project's IAM policy.
options.B: Cloud Asset Inventory's list of service accounts in the project.
options.C: The Admin Activity logs for the last 30 days.
options.D: deploy-sa's own IAM policy, plus project grants of those roles.

explanation.summary: A service account is both an identity and a resource. What it can do is in the policies of the resources it accesses; who can use it is in its own IAM policy — and in higher-level grants of roles such as Service Account User and Token Creator, which apply to every service account below.

option_breakdown.A: That shows what deploy-sa can do, not who can act as it.
option_breakdown.B: A list of accounts says nothing about who can use them.
option_breakdown.C: Logs show who did use it, not who can.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Its own resource policy, plus inherited grants.

questions.title: Running every gcloud command as a service account
questions.summary: gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account makes all commands impersonate one service account.
questions.question: An administrator holds Token Creator on the tf-admin service account and wants every gcloud command in their session to run as tf-admin, without downloading a key and without adding a flag to each command. What should they do?

options.A: Run gcloud auth activate-service-account with a new key for tf-admin.
options.B: Set the auth/impersonate_service_account gcloud property.
options.C: Export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS pointing at their user credentials file.
options.D: Add tf-admin to the administrator's Google group.

explanation.summary: With auth/impersonate_service_account set, gcloud uses the administrator's credentials to request short-lived tokens for the service account on every call. Audit logs record both identities. The per-command equivalent is --impersonate-service-account.

option_breakdown.A: That needs a long-lived key, which the requirement rules out.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Impersonation for every command, with short-lived tokens.
option_breakdown.C: That changes Application Default Credentials for libraries, and still as the user.
option_breakdown.D: Service accounts cannot be group members for sign-in purposes; this grants nothing.

questions.title: Using a federated identity from application code
questions.summary: A WIF credential configuration file tells client libraries how to exchange the external token; it holds no secret.
questions.question: A workload pool and an OIDC provider are set up for an on-premises application that can obtain tokens from the company's identity provider. The application uses Google Cloud client libraries with Application Default Credentials. What must you give the application?

options.A: A service account key file for the service account it will impersonate.
options.B: The provider's client secret, embedded in the source code.
options.C: A credential configuration file for the provider, used by ADC.
options.D: A gcloud user login performed once on the server.

explanation.summary: The credential configuration file describes where to get the external token and how to exchange it (and, optionally, which service account to impersonate). It contains no secret, and client libraries use it through Application Default Credentials.

option_breakdown.A: A key is the long-lived secret that federation replaces.
option_breakdown.B: There is no client secret to embed; the external IdP issues the token.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The non-secret configuration that ADC uses to federate.
option_breakdown.D: A person's login is not a workload identity and expires.

questions.title: Two scripts editing the same policy at once
questions.summary: set-iam-policy uses the policy's etag, so a concurrent change makes the second write fail instead of overwriting it.
questions.question: Two automation jobs each read a project's IAM policy with get-iam-policy, add a different binding locally, and write it back with set-iam-policy a few seconds apart. The second write is rejected. What happened, and what should the second job do?

options.A: The etag changed; re-read the policy, re-apply, and write again.
options.B: The second job lacks permission; grant it Project IAM Admin.
options.C: IAM allows only one policy change per hour; wait and retry.
options.D: The policy exceeded its size limit; remove unused bindings.

explanation.summary: Each policy carries an etag; set-iam-policy with a stale etag fails, which prevents one job from silently overwriting the other's binding. The fix is read-modify-write again (or use add-iam-policy-binding).

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Each policy carries an etag; set-iam-policy with a stale etag fails, which prevents one job from silently overwriting the other's binding. The fix is read-modify-write again (or use add-iam-policy-binding).
option_breakdown.B: It already wrote a policy seconds ago; permissions are not the issue.
option_breakdown.C: There is no hourly limit on policy changes.
option_breakdown.D: A size limit produces a different error and was not approached by one binding.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud projects get-iam-policy P --format=json > policy.json   # includes "etag"
gcloud projects set-iam-policy P policy.json

questions.title: Production admin rights only during an incident
questions.summary: Privileged Access Manager grants time-bound, approved, audited elevation on request.
questions.question: SREs must not hold standing admin rights in production. During an incident, an on-call SRE should be able to request Compute Admin on the production project for up to four hours, with a second SRE approving, and lose it automatically afterwards. What should you configure?

options.A: A standing roles/compute.admin grant to the SRE group, reviewed every quarter.
options.B: An IAM condition on roles/compute.admin limited to office hours.
options.C: A Privileged Access Manager entitlement, approved, for up to 4 hours.
options.D: A shared break-glass user account whose password is kept in a safe.

explanation.summary: Privileged Access Manager defines who may request which role on which resource, for how long and with whose approval, and removes the grant when it expires — all audited.

option_breakdown.A: A standing grant is exactly what the requirement forbids.
option_breakdown.B: A time-of-day condition is standing access within those hours, with no request or approval.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Privileged Access Manager defines who may request which role on which resource, for how long and with whose approval, and removes the grant when it expires — all audited.
option_breakdown.D: A shared account removes individual attribution and is a long-lived secret.

questions.title: A role that applies only to resources tagged env=dev
questions.summary: An IAM condition with resource.matchTag limits a grant to resources carrying a tag value.
questions.question: Developers need roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1 in a shared project, but only on VMs tagged env=dev (a resource-manager tag), never on the production VMs in the same project. What should you do?

options.A: A conditional grant using resource.matchTag for env=dev.
options.B: Grant the role on the project and ask developers to leave production VMs alone.
options.C: Add a network tag dev to the development VMs and grant the role on the tag.
options.D: Grant the role with a condition on the label env=dev.

explanation.summary: Conditional IAM can test resource-manager tags with resource.matchTag, so the grant is effective only on resources that carry env=dev.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Conditional IAM can test resource-manager tags with resource.matchTag, so the grant is effective only on resources that carry env=dev.
option_breakdown.B: An unconditional grant covers every VM in the project, including production.
option_breakdown.C: Network tags are firewall and route selectors; IAM cannot be granted on them.
option_breakdown.D: Labels are not available to IAM conditions; tags are the IAM-governed metadata.

questions.title: Network builders who must not touch firewalls
questions.summary: compute.networkAdmin manages networks, subnets and routes but not firewall rules; compute.securityAdmin does firewalls.
questions.question: A company separates duties: the network team builds VPCs, subnets, routes and load balancers, while only the security team may create or change firewall rules and SSL certificates. Which predefined role should the network team get?

options.A: roles/compute.securityAdmin
options.B: roles/compute.admin
options.C: roles/editor
options.D: roles/compute.networkAdmin

explanation.summary: Compute Network Admin covers networking resources but explicitly excludes firewall rules and SSL certificates, which belong to Compute Security Admin.

option_breakdown.A: Security Admin is the role for firewalls and certificates — the security team's role.
option_breakdown.B: Compute Admin includes firewall rules, breaking the separation.
option_breakdown.C: Editor spans every service, firewalls included.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Compute Network Admin covers networking resources but explicitly excludes firewall rules and SSL certificates, which belong to Compute Security Admin.

questions.title: Calling an IAP-protected app from a script
questions.summary: An OIDC ID token for a service account, minted with the correct audience, authenticates to IAP or Cloud Run.
questions.question: A nightly script, running as a user who may impersonate report-bot@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com, must call an internal web app protected by IAP. IAP expects an OIDC token whose audience is the app's OAuth client ID. What should the script obtain?

options.A: An OAuth access token for report-bot from gcloud auth print-access-token.
options.B: A JSON key for report-bot, passed in an Authorization header.
options.C: The user's own password, sent with basic authentication.
options.D: An ID token for report-bot with that audience, by impersonation.

explanation.summary: IAP and Cloud Run authenticate callers with OIDC ID tokens for a specific audience; impersonation mints one for the service account with no key.

option_breakdown.A: An access token is for calling Google APIs; IAP expects an ID token with the right audience.
option_breakdown.B: A key is a long-lived secret and is not itself a bearer token.
option_breakdown.C: IAP does not accept passwords.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. IAP and Cloud Run authenticate callers with OIDC ID tokens for a specific audience; impersonation mints one for the service account with no key.

questions.title: Signed URLs with no key file
questions.summary: A signed URL can be signed through impersonation (signBlob), with no service-account key.
questions.question: A backend on Cloud Run issues signed URLs for private objects. The organisation policy forbids service-account keys. The service runs as web@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com. How can it sign the URLs?

options.A: Sign through the IAM Credentials signBlob API as web@.
options.B: Create a key for web@ as an exception to the policy.
options.C: Make the objects public and share the plain URLs.
options.D: Use an HMAC key belonging to a user account.

explanation.summary: The IAM Service Account Credentials API signs data with a Google-managed key; a service with Token Creator on its own account can sign URLs without any key file.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The IAM Service Account Credentials API signs data with a Google-managed key; a service with Token Creator on its own account can sign URLs without any key file.
option_breakdown.B: An exception defeats the policy, and a key is exactly the long-lived secret to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Public objects remove the time limit and the privacy signed URLs provide.
option_breakdown.D: A user's HMAC key ties production signing to a person and is still a stored secret.

questions.title: An access token that must last eight hours
questions.summary: Access tokens last one hour by default; up to 12 hours needs the credential-lifetime organisation policy.
questions.question: A long-running data transfer tool can refresh its token only at start-up and needs an access token for a service account valid for eight hours. Requests for more than 3600 seconds are rejected. What must be configured?

options.A: Nothing; request a longer lifetime with --lifetime and it is granted automatically.
options.B: List the account in the lifetime extension constraint, then ask.
options.C: Create a service-account key, which produces tokens that never expire.
options.D: Grant roles/owner to the service account.

explanation.summary: Access tokens are capped at one hour unless the service account is listed in the credential lifetime extension constraint, which permits up to 12 hours.

option_breakdown.A: Without the constraint, lifetimes above one hour are rejected — as observed.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Access tokens are capped at one hour unless the service account is listed in the credential lifetime extension constraint, which permits up to 12 hours.
option_breakdown.C: Tokens from a key also last an hour; the key itself is the long-lived secret to avoid.
option_breakdown.D: Roles do not change token lifetime.

questions.title: A JWT for a partner API, signed without a key
questions.summary: The IAM Credentials signJwt method signs a JWT with a service account's Google-managed key.
questions.question: A partner API accepts requests carrying a JWT signed by one of your service accounts, whose public keys it fetches from Google. Your Cloud Run service must produce such JWTs, and service-account keys are forbidden. What should it do?

options.A: Create a service-account key and sign the JWTs locally.
options.B: Send the partner an OAuth access token instead of a JWT.
options.C: Call the IAM Credentials signJwt method as that service account.
options.D: Store a private key in Secret Manager and sign with it.

explanation.summary: signJwt signs a JWT with the service account's Google-managed private key, so no key material ever leaves Google; the caller needs Token Creator on the account.

option_breakdown.A: A key is exactly what is forbidden.
option_breakdown.B: The partner expects a signed JWT it can verify, not a Google access token.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. signJwt signs a JWT with the service account's Google-managed private key, so no key material ever leaves Google; the caller needs Token Creator on the account.
option_breakdown.D: A stored private key is still a long-lived secret.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam service-accounts sign-jwt claims.json signed.jwt \
  --iam-account=partner-caller@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com

questions.title: A host-network Pod that ignores Workload Identity
questions.summary: Pods that use the host network cannot use Workload Identity Federation for GKE; they see the node's identity.
questions.question: Workload Identity Federation for GKE is enabled on a cluster and its node pools, and most Pods use their Kubernetes service accounts correctly. One monitoring DaemonSet, which sets hostNetwork: true, still calls Google APIs as the node's service account. Why?

options.A: DaemonSets are not supported by Kubernetes service accounts.
options.B: The DaemonSet's namespace needs its own workload identity pool.
options.C: Host-network Pods can't use it, so they get the node's identity.
options.D: The node pool must be recreated after every DaemonSet change.

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Federation for GKE does not apply to Pods using the host network; such a Pod needs a different design (for example, not using hostNetwork) to get its own identity.

option_breakdown.A: DaemonSet Pods use service accounts like any other Pod.
option_breakdown.B: A cluster has one workload identity pool, PROJECT.svc.id.goog, for every namespace.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Workload Identity Federation for GKE does not apply to Pods using the host network; such a Pod needs a different design (for example, not using hostNetwork) to get its own identity.
option_breakdown.D: Node pools are not recreated for workload changes.

questions.title: Linking a Kubernetes service account to an IAM service account
questions.summary: Grant roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser to PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NS/KSA] on the IAM SA and annotate the KSA.
questions.question: Pods in namespace media run as Kubernetes service account uploader and must act as the existing IAM service account media-sa@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com, which already holds the roles they need. What two steps are required?

options.A: A workloadIdentityUser grant for media/uploader, plus a KSA annotation.
options.B: Create a key for media-sa and mount it into the Pods as a Secret.
options.C: Grant roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on media-sa to the node pool's service account.
options.D: Annotate the node pool with media-sa's email.

explanation.summary: The IAM binding lets that one Kubernetes service account impersonate media-sa, and the annotation tells GKE which account to exchange its tokens for.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The IAM binding lets that one Kubernetes service account impersonate media-sa, and the annotation tells GKE which account to exchange its tokens for.
option_breakdown.B: A mounted key is what Workload Identity Federation exists to remove.
option_breakdown.C: Granting the node's account gives the access to every Pod on the node.
option_breakdown.D: The mapping is per Kubernetes service account, not per node pool.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding media-sa@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member="serviceAccount:P.svc.id.goog[media/uploader]"
kubectl annotate serviceaccount uploader -n media \
  iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=media-sa@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com

questions.title: The same Pod works in one namespace but not another
questions.summary: A Workload Identity principal names the namespace and KSA, so a copy in another namespace is a different principal.
questions.question: A Pod running as Kubernetes service account reader in namespace prod reads a bucket successfully through a direct IAM grant. The identical Deployment in namespace staging, also with a KSA called reader, gets 403. Why?

options.A: Workload Identity Federation works in only one namespace per cluster.
options.B: The grant names prod's reader; staging's reader is another principal.
options.C: The staging Pods run on different nodes whose service account lacks access.
options.D: Bucket permissions take 24 hours to reach a second namespace.

explanation.summary: The principal identifier includes the namespace and the Kubernetes service account name, so each namespace's KSA must be granted separately.

option_breakdown.A: Every namespace can use Workload Identity Federation.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The principal identifier includes the namespace and the Kubernetes service account name, so each namespace's KSA must be granted separately.
option_breakdown.C: With Workload Identity, access comes from the Pod's KSA, not the node's account.
option_breakdown.D: IAM changes propagate in minutes, and none was made for staging.

questions.title: Custom node account pulling from another project
questions.summary: A custom node service account needs Artifact Registry Reader on a repository in another project to pull from it.
questions.question: A cluster's nodes run as gke-nodes@app-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com, which holds only roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount. Logs and metrics flow, but Pods using images from a repository in project shared-images fail with ImagePullBackOff and a 403. What should you grant?

options.A: roles/artifactregistry.reader to each Pod's Kubernetes service account.
options.B: Artifact Registry Reader for gke-nodes@ on the shared repository.
options.C: roles/editor to gke-nodes@ in app-prod.
options.D: roles/artifactregistry.admin to gke-nodes@ on the organisation.

explanation.summary: Images are pulled by the node, as the node service account; for a repository in another project that account needs Artifact Registry Reader on the repository (or its project).

option_breakdown.A: Image pulls do not use the Pod's identity, so Workload Identity grants do not help here.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Images are pulled by the node, as the node service account; for a repository in another project that account needs Artifact Registry Reader on the repository (or its project).
option_breakdown.C: Editor in app-prod grants nothing in shared-images and is far too broad.
option_breakdown.D: Admin across the organisation is far beyond read access to one repository.

questions.title: An AWS workload reading from Google Cloud
questions.summary: An AWS provider in a workload identity pool accepts AWS roles, exchanged for short-lived Google tokens.
questions.question: An application on Amazon EC2 runs under an IAM role and must read a BigQuery dataset in Google Cloud. Service-account keys are prohibited. What should you configure?

options.A: A workload identity pool with an AWS provider, granted to the role.
options.B: A service-account key stored in AWS Secrets Manager.
options.C: A workforce identity pool for the AWS account.
options.D: VPC Network Peering between the AWS VPC and the Google Cloud VPC.

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Federation supports AWS as an identity provider: the workload presents its AWS credentials to Google STS and receives short-lived Google credentials.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Workload Identity Federation supports AWS as an identity provider: the workload presents its AWS credentials to Google STS and receives short-lived Google credentials.
option_breakdown.B: A key stored elsewhere is still a long-lived key.
option_breakdown.C: Workforce pools are for people; software uses workload identity pools.
option_breakdown.D: Network connectivity does nothing for authentication, and peering connects Google VPCs.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create aws-pool --location=global
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-aws ec2 --workload-identity-pool=aws-pool \
  --location=global --account-id=123456789012

questions.title: An Azure workload calling Google Cloud
questions.summary: Workloads on Azure federate through an OIDC provider that trusts the Entra ID tenant's issuer.
questions.question: An application on an Azure VM uses a managed identity and must write to a Cloud Storage bucket. Service-account keys are prohibited. What should you configure in Google Cloud?

options.A: A workload identity pool with an OIDC provider for the Azure issuer.
options.B: A workforce identity pool for the Azure tenant.
options.C: A service-account key stored in Azure Key Vault.
options.D: An AWS provider in a workload identity pool.

explanation.summary: Azure managed identities obtain tokens from Microsoft Entra ID; an OIDC provider trusting that issuer lets the workload exchange them for short-lived Google credentials.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Azure managed identities obtain tokens from Microsoft Entra ID; an OIDC provider trusting that issuer lets the workload exchange them for short-lived Google credentials.
option_breakdown.B: Workforce pools are for people signing in, not workloads.
option_breakdown.C: A key in another cloud's vault is still a long-lived key.
option_breakdown.D: The AWS provider type validates AWS credentials, not Azure tokens.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc azure --workload-identity-pool=multicloud \
  --location=global --issuer-uri=https://sts.windows.net/TENANT_ID/ \
  --allowed-audiences=APP_ID_URI --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub"

questions.title: Who may create pools and providers
questions.summary: Workload Identity Pool Admin manages pools and providers; it is separate from using them.
questions.question: A platform engineer must create and maintain workload identity pools and providers in project idp-hub, but must not be able to grant themselves access to other resources. Which role fits best?

options.A: roles/owner on idp-hub.
options.B: roles/iam.workloadIdentityPoolAdmin on idp-hub.
options.C: roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser on every service account in idp-hub.
options.D: roles/iam.securityAdmin at the organisation.

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Pool Admin manages pools and providers without granting rights to set IAM policies on other resources.

option_breakdown.A: Owner lets the engineer grant themselves anything in the project.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Workload Identity Pool Admin manages pools and providers without granting rights to set IAM policies on other resources.
option_breakdown.C: Workload Identity User lets principals impersonate service accounts; it does not create pools.
option_breakdown.D: Security Admin can set IAM policies across the organisation — far too broad.

questions.title: On-premises servers with certificates but no IdP
questions.summary: Workload Identity Federation can trust X.509 certificates issued by your own CA.
questions.question: On-premises batch servers have no OIDC or SAML identity provider, but each holds a client certificate issued by the company's internal certificate authority. They must call Google Cloud APIs without service-account keys. What should you configure?

options.A: A workload identity pool with an X.509 provider trusting the CA.
options.B: A service-account key per server, rotated monthly.
options.C: An OIDC provider pointing at the certificate authority's web page.
options.D: Workforce Identity Federation for each server's hostname.

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Federation supports X.509 certificate-based federation: workloads authenticate with certificates chained to a trust store you configure, and receive short-lived Google credentials.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Workload Identity Federation supports X.509 certificate-based federation: workloads authenticate with certificates chained to a trust store you configure, and receive short-lived Google credentials.
option_breakdown.B: Rotated keys are still long-lived secrets on disk.
option_breakdown.C: A CA is not an OIDC issuer; the provider type must match the credential.
option_breakdown.D: Workforce federation is for people signing in, not servers.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-x509 onprem-ca --workload-identity-pool=onprem \
  --location=global --trust-store-config-path=trust_store.yaml \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.subject.dn.cn"

questions.title: Granting a key role to a service agent that does not exist yet
questions.summary: Force-create a service agent with gcloud beta services identity create before its first use.
questions.question: A Terraform pipeline at Quarrydale Systems creates a new project and must grant the Pub/Sub service agent Encrypter/Decrypter on a Cloud KMS key before the first CMEK-protected topic is created. The grant fails because the service agent does not exist yet. What should the pipeline do first?

options.A: Provision the Pub/Sub service agent on demand first.
options.B: Create a user-managed service account named like the Pub/Sub service agent.
options.C: Grant the key role to the project's default Compute Engine service account instead.
options.D: Wait 24 hours for the service agent to appear on its own.

explanation.summary: services identity create provisions the product's Google-managed service agent on demand, so it can be granted roles before the service first uses it.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. services identity create provisions the product's Google-managed service agent on demand, so it can be granted roles before the service first uses it.
option_breakdown.B: Service agents live in Google-managed domains; you cannot create one yourself.
option_breakdown.C: The Compute Engine account is not the identity Pub/Sub uses for the key.
option_breakdown.D: Agents are created on first use or on request, not after a delay.

questions.title: Restoring a service account deleted last week
questions.summary: A deleted service account can be undeleted within 30 days using its unique ID, keeping its bindings.
questions.question: A service account used by a batch job was deleted by mistake eight days ago and the job now fails. Its role bindings in several projects were never removed. What restores the job with the least rework?

options.A: Create a new service account with the same name.
options.B: Create a new service account with a different name and re-grant every role.
options.C: Undelete the service account by its unique ID.
options.D: Nothing can be done; deletion is permanent.

explanation.summary: Deleted service accounts can be undeleted for 30 days by unique ID, returning the same principal the existing bindings refer to.

option_breakdown.A: A new account with the same name is a different principal, so the old bindings do not apply to it.
option_breakdown.B: It works, but it means re-creating every grant when undeleting restores them.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Deleted service accounts can be undeleted for 30 days by unique ID, returning the same principal the existing bindings refer to.
option_breakdown.D: The 30-day undelete window has not passed.

questions.title: Renaming a service account
questions.summary: A service account's email (its ID) is permanent; only the display name and description can change.
questions.question: A service account was created as tmp-test@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com and is now used in production. The team wants its email to read orders-prod@. What must they do?

options.A: Run gcloud iam service-accounts update with a new account ID.
options.B: Change the display name, which changes the email address.
options.C: Create orders-prod, move roles and workloads, then retire the old one.
options.D: Rename the project, which renames every service account in it.

explanation.summary: The account ID in a service account's email cannot be changed after creation; a new account and a migration are required.

option_breakdown.A: update changes the display name and description, not the ID.
option_breakdown.B: The display name is a label; the email stays the same.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The account ID in a service account's email cannot be changed after creation; a new account and a migration are required.
option_breakdown.D: Service-account emails use the project ID, which never changes, not the project's display name.

questions.title: Who acted through a service account
questions.summary: Audit log entries for impersonated calls record the original caller in serviceAccountDelegationInfo.
questions.question: Several engineers can impersonate deploy-sa. Last night a firewall rule was deleted by deploy-sa. Security must find which engineer did it. Where is that recorded?

options.A: In the deletion's audit log entry, under its delegation information.
options.B: Nowhere; impersonated calls are attributed only to the service account.
options.C: In the service account's key list.
options.D: In the VPC Flow Logs for the network.

explanation.summary: When a principal impersonates a service account, the audit log records both the service account and the original principal in the delegation chain.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. When a principal impersonates a service account, the audit log records both the service account and the original principal in the delegation chain.
option_breakdown.B: Impersonation keeps attribution — that is one of its advantages over shared keys.
option_breakdown.C: Impersonation uses no keys, and key lists do not record actions.
option_breakdown.D: Flow logs record network traffic, not API calls.

questions.title: A build trigger that runs as a chosen service account
questions.summary: Choosing a service account for a Cloud Build trigger requires actAs (Service Account User) on it.
questions.question: A developer creates a Cloud Build trigger configured to run builds as builder@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com and gets a permission error mentioning iam.serviceAccounts.actAs. What should they be granted?

options.A: roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on builder@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com.
options.B: roles/cloudbuild.builds.editor on the organisation.
options.C: roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin on builder@.
options.D: roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser on builder@.

explanation.summary: Configuring a resource to run as a service account requires actAs on that account, which Service Account User provides.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Configuring a resource to run as a service account requires actAs on that account, which Service Account User provides.
option_breakdown.B: The error is about acting as the account, not about build permissions, and an organisation grant is too broad.
option_breakdown.C: Key administration manages keys, which are not needed and should not exist.
option_breakdown.D: Workload Identity User is for federated and GKE identities impersonating the account.

questions.title: ID tokens only, not access tokens
questions.summary: roles/iam.serviceAccountOpenIdTokenCreator lets a caller mint OIDC ID tokens but not OAuth access tokens.
questions.question: A scheduler identity only needs to mint OIDC ID tokens as invoker@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com to call a private Cloud Run service. It must not be able to obtain OAuth access tokens that call Google APIs as invoker. Which role should it get on invoker@?

options.A: roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator
options.B: roles/iam.serviceAccountUser
options.C: roles/iam.serviceAccountOpenIdTokenCreator
options.D: roles/run.admin

explanation.summary: Service Account OpenID Connect Identity Token Creator permits generating ID tokens only, which is exactly what calling Cloud Run needs.

option_breakdown.A: Token Creator also allows access tokens and signing, which the requirement excludes.
option_breakdown.B: Service Account User lets the caller attach the account to resources; it does not mint tokens.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Service Account OpenID Connect Identity Token Creator permits generating ID tokens only, which is exactly what calling Cloud Run needs.
option_breakdown.D: Run Admin manages Cloud Run services; it mints no tokens and is far broader.

questions.title: Managing one service account, not all of them
questions.summary: Roles granted on a single service account resource apply to that account only.
questions.question: The data team must be able to update the description of, disable and re-enable the service account etl@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com, but no other service account in project P. What should you grant?

options.A: roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin on project P.
options.B: roles/editor on project P.
options.C: roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on project P.
options.D: roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin on etl@ only.

explanation.summary: A service account is a resource, so a role granted on it covers that one account; Service Account Admin there allows updating, disabling and enabling it.

option_breakdown.A: A project grant covers every service account in P.
option_breakdown.B: Editor is broad and covers every service in the project.
option_breakdown.C: Service Account User allows attaching accounts to resources, not administering them — and project-wide.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A service account is a resource, so a role granted on it covers that one account; Service Account Admin there allows updating, disabling and enabling it.

questions.title: Attaching a service account from another project
questions.summary: Attaching a service account from a different project needs actAs and the cross-project usage constraint not enforced.
questions.question: Service accounts are kept in a central project, idents. A developer with Service Account User on app@idents.iam.gserviceaccount.com tries to create a VM in project app-prod that runs as it, and gets an error that cross-project service account usage is disabled. What must change?

options.A: The developer needs roles/owner on idents.
options.B: Stop enforcing iam.disableCrossProjectServiceAccountUsage on idents.
options.C: The service account must be moved into app-prod.
options.D: The VM must be created with a service-account key instead.

explanation.summary: By default, organisations can block attaching a service account to resources in other projects; the boolean constraint must be relaxed on the project that owns the service account.

option_breakdown.A: The developer already holds actAs; the organisation policy is what blocks it.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. By default, organisations can block attaching a service account to resources in other projects; the boolean constraint must be relaxed on the project that owns the service account.
option_breakdown.C: Service accounts cannot be moved between projects.
option_breakdown.D: Keys are the long-lived secret this design avoids, and do not attach an identity to a VM.

questions.title: A VM denied despite the right IAM role
questions.summary: Legacy access scopes limit what a VM's service account can do, on top of IAM.
questions.question: A VM runs as app@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com, which holds roles/pubsub.publisher. Publishing from the VM fails with an insufficient-scopes error. The VM was created with the default access scopes. What should you do?

options.A: Grant app@ the Owner role on the project.
options.B: Create a key for app@ and use it on the VM.
options.C: Restart the Pub/Sub API in the project.
options.D: Stop the VM, set the cloud-platform scope, and start it again.

explanation.summary: Access scopes are a VM-level filter applied on top of IAM; the default scopes exclude Pub/Sub, and scopes can be changed only while the VM is stopped. The recommended pattern is cloud-platform plus narrow IAM roles.

option_breakdown.A: More IAM roles do not help while the scope blocks the API.
option_breakdown.B: A key sidesteps scopes but introduces a long-lived secret.
option_breakdown.C: APIs are not restarted, and the error names scopes.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Access scopes are a VM-level filter applied on top of IAM; the default scopes exclude Pub/Sub, and scopes can be changed only while the VM is stopped. The recommended pattern is cloud-platform plus narrow IAM roles.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances stop vm1 --zone=Z
gcloud compute instances set-service-account vm1 --zone=Z \
  --service-account=app@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com --scopes=cloud-platform
gcloud compute instances start vm1 --zone=Z

questions.title: Consuming from one subscription only
questions.summary: Grant Pub/Sub Subscriber on the single subscription rather than on the project.
questions.question: A worker's service account must pull messages from the subscription orders-worker. The project has forty other subscriptions it must not read. Where should roles/pubsub.subscriber be granted?

options.A: On the project.
options.B: On the topic that feeds the subscription.
options.C: On the orders-worker subscription.
options.D: On the organisation.

explanation.summary: Pub/Sub supports IAM on individual subscriptions, so the grant can cover exactly the one the worker consumes.

option_breakdown.A: A project grant lets the worker read all forty other subscriptions.
option_breakdown.B: Topic-level permissions do not grant pulling from a subscription.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Pub/Sub supports IAM on individual subscriptions, so the grant can cover exactly the one the worker consumes.
option_breakdown.D: An organisation grant is broader still.

questions.title: A federated pipeline that must act as a service account
questions.summary: Grant roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser on the service account to the federated principal set, then impersonate.
questions.question: An external CI system authenticates through a workload identity pool. One API it calls does not accept federated principals directly, so the pipeline must act as the service account deployer@ops.iam.gserviceaccount.com. What grant is required?

options.A: roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin on deployer@ so the pipeline can create a key.
options.B: roles/iam.workloadIdentityPoolAdmin on the project to the pipeline.
options.C: Workload Identity User on deployer@, for the pipeline's principal set.
options.D: roles/owner on the project to the pipeline's federated principal.

explanation.summary: With service account impersonation, the federated identity exchanges its token for the service account's short-lived credentials. That requires Workload Identity User on the service account.

option_breakdown.A: Keys are exactly what federation avoids.
option_breakdown.B: Pool Admin manages pools and providers; it does not let a workload act as a service account.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. With service account impersonation, the federated identity exchanges its token for the service account's short-lived credentials. That requires Workload Identity User on the service account.
option_breakdown.D: Owner is excessive and still does not grant impersonation of the account.

questions.title: Federating a Kubernetes cluster whose issuer is private
questions.summary: Upload the cluster's JWKS to the OIDC provider (--jwk-json-path) when Google cannot fetch the issuer's keys.
questions.question: Workloads on an on-premises Kubernetes cluster should call Google Cloud APIs using their Kubernetes service account tokens. The cluster's OIDC issuer URL is reachable only inside the corporate network. How should you configure the workload identity pool provider?

options.A: Expose the Kubernetes API server to the internet so Google can fetch the keys.
options.B: Create an X.509 provider using the cluster's CA certificate.
options.C: Create a SAML provider using the cluster's service account signing key.
options.D: An OIDC provider with the issuer URI and the uploaded cluster JWKS.

explanation.summary: When the issuer's keys cannot be fetched from the internet, you upload the JWKS to the provider. Google then verifies the tokens without reaching the cluster.

option_breakdown.A: Exposing the control plane is unnecessary and risky.
option_breakdown.B: X.509 federation authenticates with client certificates, not Kubernetes service account tokens.
option_breakdown.C: Kubernetes service account tokens are OIDC JWTs, not SAML assertions.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. When the issuer's keys cannot be fetched from the internet, you upload the JWKS to the provider. Google then verifies the tokens without reaching the cluster.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl get --raw /openid/v1/jwks > cluster-jwks.json
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc onprem-k8s --location=global \
  --workload-identity-pool=k8s --issuer-uri=ISSUER \
  --attribute-mapping=google.subject=assertion.sub --jwk-json-path=cluster-jwks.json

questions.title: Keeping a team's identities inside its own projects
questions.summary: Principal access boundary policies limit which resources principals are eligible to access, whatever they are granted.
questions.question: Security wants to guarantee that users in the contractors group can never use any Google Cloud resource outside the contractors folder, even if someone elsewhere mistakenly grants them a role. What should you use?

options.A: An IAM deny policy on every other folder, updated as folders are added.
options.B: Remove the group's bindings outside the folder every week.
options.C: A principal access boundary policy limiting them to the folder.
options.D: An organisation policy that restricts resource locations.

explanation.summary: Principal access boundary policies define which resources a set of principals is eligible to access. They cannot grant access, but they block access to anything outside the boundary regardless of role grants.

option_breakdown.A: Deny policies attach to resources; covering every current and future folder is fragile.
option_breakdown.B: Periodic clean-up leaves a window in which a mistaken grant works.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Principal access boundary policies define which resources a set of principals is eligible to access. They cannot grant access, but they block access to anything outside the boundary regardless of role grants.
option_breakdown.D: Location restrictions govern where resources are created, not who can use them.

explanation.gcloud_command:
# PAB policy with a rule listing //cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/folders/CONTRACTORS_FOLDER,
# bound to principalSet://cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/... for the contractors' principals

questions.title: Access only during business hours
questions.summary: An IAM condition on request.time limits when a role binding is effective.
questions.question: An offshore support group may use Compute Instance Admin on the support project only on weekdays between 08:00 and 18:00 Warsaw time. Outside those hours the permissions must not work. What should you grant?

options.A: The role with an expiry condition at the end of each day.
options.B: The role with no condition, plus a Cloud Scheduler job that adds and removes it twice a day.
options.C: The role with an IAM condition on request.time for weekdays 08:00–18:00 in Europe/Warsaw.
options.D: A custom role that excludes compute.instances.delete.

explanation.summary: IAM conditions can test the request's date and time with a time zone, so the binding is effective only in the allowed window.

option_breakdown.A: A single expiry time ends access permanently after one day.
option_breakdown.B: Scripted grant changes are fragile and leave gaps or overlaps if a job fails.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. IAM conditions can test the request's date and time with a time zone, so the binding is effective only in the allowed window.
option_breakdown.D: Removing one permission does not restrict when access works.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding support-prj --member=group:offshore@example.com \
  --role=roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1 --condition='title=business-hours,expression=
  request.time.getHours("Europe/Warsaw") >= 8 && request.time.getHours("Europe/Warsaw") < 18 &&
  request.time.getDayOfWeek("Europe/Warsaw") >= 1 && request.time.getDayOfWeek("Europe/Warsaw") <= 5'

questions.title: Letting a team grant only a few roles
questions.summary: A condition on setIamPolicy using modifiedGrantsByRole limits which roles a delegate may grant.
questions.question: A project's team lead should be able to grant and revoke only roles/logging.viewer and roles/monitoring.viewer to colleagues, and never any other role. What should you grant the team lead?

options.A: roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin with no condition.
options.B: Project IAM Admin, with a condition limiting grants to those two roles.
options.C: roles/owner on the project.
options.D: roles/logging.admin and roles/monitoring.admin.

explanation.summary: IAM conditions can use the API attribute iam.googleapis.com/modifiedGrantsByRole to restrict which roles a policy change may add or remove, which delegates granting safely.

option_breakdown.A: Unconditioned Project IAM Admin can grant any role, including Owner.
