option_breakdown.B: Correct. IAM conditions can use the API attribute iam.googleapis.com/modifiedGrantsByRole to restrict which roles a policy change may add or remove, which delegates granting safely.
option_breakdown.C: Owner grants far more than needed.
option_breakdown.D: Admin roles on those products do not allow granting IAM roles.

questions.title: Access to every bucket whose name starts with logs-
questions.summary: An IAM condition on resource.name.startsWith scopes a project-level grant to matching buckets.
questions.question: A log-shipping service account needs to write objects to the 30 buckets in a project whose names begin with logs-, and to no other bucket. New logs- buckets are created every month. What should you grant?

options.A: Storage Object Creator on each bucket, updated monthly.
options.B: Storage Admin on the project.
options.C: Storage Object Creator on the project with no condition.
options.D: Object Creator on the project, conditioned on the logs- name prefix.

explanation.summary: A resource-name condition makes the project-level grant apply only to buckets (and their objects) with the matching prefix, including buckets created later.

option_breakdown.A: Per-bucket grants work but must be updated for each new bucket.
option_breakdown.B: Storage Admin is far broader than writing objects.
option_breakdown.C: Without a condition the account can write to every bucket.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A resource-name condition makes the project-level grant apply only to buckets (and their objects) with the matching prefix, including buckets created later.

questions.title: Reviewing IAM policies across the organisation without data access
questions.summary: Security Reviewer grants permission to list and get IAM policies on all resources, not to read data.
questions.question: An internal auditor must be able to read the IAM policy of every organisation, folder, project and resource in the organisation, but must not read any data or change anything. Which predefined role should you grant at the organisation?

options.A: roles/viewer
options.B: roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin
options.C: roles/iam.roleViewer
options.D: roles/iam.securityReviewer

explanation.summary: Security Reviewer includes the permissions to list and get IAM policies across resources, without data access or change rights.

option_breakdown.A: Viewer includes read access to much resource data and not every IAM policy.
option_breakdown.B: Organization Admin can change IAM policies.
option_breakdown.C: Role Viewer shows role definitions, not who holds them.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Security Reviewer includes the permissions to list and get IAM policies across resources, without data access or change rights.

questions.title: An IAM policy that has grown too large
questions.summary: Allow policies have a principal limit (1,500); consolidate individual users into groups.
questions.question: Adding one more user to a project's IAM policy fails because the policy has reached its size limit: about 1,500 individual user bindings accumulated over the years. What is the right fix?

options.A: Split the project into two projects.
options.B: Create a custom role that contains the permissions of every existing role.
options.C: Grant roles to Google groups instead of individual users.
options.D: Ask support to raise the policy limit.

explanation.summary: An allow policy can contain a limited number of principals. Groups count as one principal each and are the recommended way to manage access for many people.

option_breakdown.A: Splitting projects is disruptive and avoids the real problem.
option_breakdown.B: Fewer roles do not reduce the number of principals.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An allow policy can contain a limited number of principals. Groups count as one principal each and are the recommended way to manage access for many people.
option_breakdown.D: The limit cannot be raised.

questions.title: Keeping production and staging pipelines apart
questions.summary: Separate workload identity pools per environment keep federated identities from crossing environments.
questions.question: The same external CI system deploys to staging and production projects. Security wants a compromised staging pipeline to be unable to obtain any identity in production, with the separation visible in the configuration. What design fits?

options.A: One pool with one provider, and a naming convention on service accounts.
options.B: One pool, with a service account key for production stored in the CI secret store.
options.C: One pool granted roles/owner in both projects.
options.D: Separate workload identity pools per environment, each granted only there.

explanation.summary: Pools are the unit of trust and administration. Separate pools with their own conditions and grants keep each environment's federated identities isolated.

option_breakdown.A: A naming convention is not a security boundary.
option_breakdown.B: A production key in the CI secret store is exactly what a compromised staging pipeline could read.
option_breakdown.C: Owner in both projects is the opposite of isolation.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Pools are the unit of trust and administration. Separate pools with their own conditions and grants keep each environment's federated identities isolated.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create ci-prod --location=global --project=idp-prod
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create ci-staging --location=global --project=idp-staging

questions.title: Stopping an external workload's federation during an incident
questions.summary: Disable the workload identity provider (or pool) to stop new token exchanges immediately.
questions.question: An external CI provider reports that its OIDC signing keys may be compromised. You must immediately stop any token exchange through the provider for it, without deleting the configuration. What should you do?

options.A: Rotate the service account keys used by the pipeline.
options.B: Remove roles/iam.workloadIdentityPoolAdmin from the administrators.
options.C: Shorten the service account's token lifetime.
options.D: Disable the workload identity pool provider for that CI system.

explanation.summary: A disabled provider cannot be used to exchange tokens, and it can be re-enabled after the incident with its configuration intact.

option_breakdown.A: Federated pipelines use no service account keys.
option_breakdown.B: Admin roles govern who manages pools, not whether exchanges happen.
option_breakdown.C: Token lifetime does not stop new exchanges.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A disabled provider cannot be used to exchange tokens, and it can be re-enabled after the incident with its configuration intact.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers update-oidc ci-provider --location=global \
  --workload-identity-pool=ci --disabled

questions.title: Seeing which external workload made a call
questions.summary: Audit logs record federated principals (and delegation) so external workloads are attributable.
questions.question: An external pipeline federated through a workload identity pool deleted a Cloud Storage bucket. Directly granted federated principals were used, with no service account. Where can you see which federated identity did it?

options.A: The Admin Activity audit log entry's authentication info.
options.B: The pipeline's service account key usage metrics.
options.C: VPC Flow Logs for the bucket.
options.D: The billing export.

explanation.summary: Audit logs record the principal that made each call. For a federated identity, that is its principal identifier from the pool, so the external workload is attributable.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Audit logs record the principal that made each call. For a federated identity, that is its principal identifier from the pool, so the external workload is attributable.
option_breakdown.B: There is no service account or key in this setup.
option_breakdown.C: Flow logs record network flows, not API callers, and buckets have no VPC traffic.
option_breakdown.D: Billing data does not record who deleted resources.

questions.title: Keys that expire on their own
questions.summary: The organisation policy iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours limits the lifetime of new keys.
questions.question: A few legacy integrations still require service account keys. Security accepts them only if every new key expires automatically within 90 days. What should you set?

options.A: An IAM condition on the service accounts that expires after 90 days.
options.B: A budget alert on the projects that use keys.
options.C: The iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours constraint, set to 2160h.
options.D: A lifecycle rule on the bucket where keys are stored.

explanation.summary: The key expiry constraint sets a maximum lifetime for newly created user-managed keys, after which they stop working.

option_breakdown.A: Conditions on bindings do not expire the keys themselves.
option_breakdown.B: Budgets are unrelated to key lifetime.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The key expiry constraint sets a maximum lifetime for newly created user-managed keys, after which they stop working.
option_breakdown.D: Keys should not be stored in buckets, and lifecycle rules do not revoke them.

questions.title: An S3-compatible tool that needs Cloud Storage access
questions.summary: Cloud Storage HMAC keys for a service account let S3-compatible tools use the XML API.
questions.question: A backup appliance can only talk to storage through the Amazon S3 API with an access key and secret. It must write to one Cloud Storage bucket. What should you create?

options.A: An HMAC key for a service account that can write to the bucket.
options.B: A service account JSON key uploaded to the appliance.
options.C: An OAuth client ID and secret.
options.D: A signed URL valid for a year.

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage's interoperability mode accepts HMAC keys, which S3-compatible tools use like access keys. Tying the HMAC key to a dedicated service account keeps access scoped and revocable.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Cloud Storage's interoperability mode accepts HMAC keys, which S3-compatible tools use like access keys. Tying the HMAC key to a dedicated service account keeps access scoped and revocable.
option_breakdown.B: S3 tools cannot use JSON keys.
option_breakdown.C: OAuth clients are for user sign-in flows.
option_breakdown.D: Signed URLs cover one object and cannot live that long when signed with V4.

questions.title: Cloud Scheduler calling a private Cloud Run service
questions.summary: Cloud Scheduler sends an OIDC token for a service account that has Cloud Run Invoker.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service requires authentication. A Cloud Scheduler job must call it every hour. How should the job authenticate?

options.A: An OIDC token for a service account holding Invoker on the service.
options.B: Allow unauthenticated invocations on the service.
options.C: Put a service account key in the job's request headers.
options.D: Configure the job to send an OAuth access token with the cloud-platform scope.

explanation.summary: Cloud Run verifies Google-signed ID (OIDC) tokens. Scheduler mints one for the chosen service account, whose Invoker role authorises the call.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Cloud Run verifies Google-signed ID (OIDC) tokens. Scheduler mints one for the chosen service account, whose Invoker role authorises the call.
option_breakdown.B: That exposes the service to everyone.
option_breakdown.C: Keys in headers are insecure and not how Cloud Run authenticates.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud Run expects an ID token for its URL, not an OAuth access token.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud scheduler jobs create http hourly-report --schedule='0 * * * *' --uri=https://report-xyz.a.run.app/run \
  --oidc-service-account-email=scheduler@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com --location=us-central1

questions.title: Workload Identity Federation on Autopilot
questions.summary: Autopilot clusters have Workload Identity Federation for GKE enabled by default.
questions.question: A team creates a new GKE Autopilot cluster and asks what it must enable before Pods can use Workload Identity Federation for GKE to call Google Cloud APIs. What is accurate?

options.A: Nothing on the cluster; grant roles to the KSA's principal.
options.B: Enable it on each node pool with --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA.
options.C: Create a node pool with the GKE metadata server enabled.
options.D: Download a key for a Google service account into a Kubernetes Secret.

explanation.summary: Autopilot clusters always have Workload Identity Federation for GKE on. You only grant IAM roles to the Kubernetes service account (directly or through a Google service account).

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Autopilot clusters always have Workload Identity Federation for GKE on. You only grant IAM roles to the Kubernetes service account (directly or through a Google service account).
option_breakdown.B: Autopilot has no user-managed node pools to configure.
option_breakdown.C: There are no node pools to create in Autopilot.
option_breakdown.D: Keys are what Workload Identity Federation replaces.

questions.title: GitHub Actions cannot get a token for federation
questions.summary: The workflow job needs permissions id-token: write so GitHub issues the OIDC token to exchange.
questions.question: A GitHub Actions workflow uses the google-github-actions/auth step with a workload identity provider. The pool, provider, attribute condition and IAM grants are correct, but the step fails because no OIDC token is available. What is missing?

options.A: A service account JSON key stored as a GitHub secret.
options.B: The id-token: write permission in the workflow or job.
options.C: roles/iam.workloadIdentityPoolAdmin for the repository.
options.D: An X.509 certificate for the runner.

explanation.summary: GitHub issues an OIDC token to a job only when the workflow grants the id-token: write permission. Without that token there is nothing to exchange with Google's Security Token Service.

option_breakdown.A: A key would sidestep federation instead of fixing it; the setup is right, and only the OIDC token is missing.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. GitHub issues an OIDC token to a job only when the workflow grants the id-token: write permission. Without that token there is nothing to exchange with Google's Security Token Service.
option_breakdown.C: Pool Admin manages configuration; it does not produce the token.
option_breakdown.D: GitHub federation uses OIDC tokens, not client certificates.

explanation.gcloud_command:
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
steps:
- uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
  with:
    workload_identity_provider: projects/NUM/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github/providers/gh

questions.title: Read-only access to Cloud Run and nothing else
questions.summary: A product's predefined viewer role grants read-only access to that product only, unlike the basic Viewer role.
questions.question: An auditor must be able to see the configuration of the Cloud Run services in a project, and nothing about its other resources. Which role should you grant on the project?

options.A: The basic Viewer role.
options.B: Cloud Run Viewer.
options.C: Cloud Run Developer.
options.D: Security Reviewer.

explanation.summary: Predefined roles are scoped to one product. Cloud Run Viewer (roles/run.viewer) reads Cloud Run resources only.

option_breakdown.A: Basic Viewer reads nearly every resource in the project, far beyond Cloud Run.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. It grants read access to Cloud Run services and nothing else.
option_breakdown.C: Developer can deploy and change services, not just view them.
option_breakdown.D: Security Reviewer reads IAM policies across resources, not Cloud Run configuration.

questions.title: One service account per workload
questions.summary: Give each workload its own user-managed service account with only the roles it needs, and attach it instead of the Compute Engine default service account.
questions.question: At Thorne Clinics, three applications on Compute Engine all run as the default compute service account, which has Editor on the project. Each application uses different APIs, and a compromise of one must not expose the others' data. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Create a user-managed service account per application, with only the roles it needs.
options.B: Attach each application's own service account to its VMs instead of the default.
options.C: Create one new service account with the Editor role and share it between all three apps.
options.D: Create keys for the default service account and give one to each application.
options.E: Keep the default service account and grant it Owner, so no application fails.

explanation.summary: A service account per workload limits each one to the access it needs, so one compromised application can't use the others' permissions. The VMs must run as those accounts rather than the default.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Separate accounts with narrow roles keep each application's access apart.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Until the VMs run as the new accounts, they still use the default account's Editor role.
option_breakdown.C: One shared account means one compromise exposes all three applications.
option_breakdown.D: Keys add long-lived secrets and leave all three with the same broad permissions.
option_breakdown.E: Owner widens access further, the opposite of what's needed.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam service-accounts create billing-app --display-name='Billing app'
gcloud compute instances set-service-account VM_NAME --zone=ZONE \
  --service-account=billing-app@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com --scopes=cloud-platform

questions.title: A service account key pushed to a public repository
questions.summary: When a key leaks, disable or delete that key at once, then check audit logs for actions made with its key ID.
questions.question: A developer at Ashcombe Retail pushed a JSON key for the order-sync service account to a public GitHub repository an hour ago. Order sync must keep running on its VMs, which use the attached service account and not the key. Which two actions should you take first? (Choose two.)

options.A: Disable or delete the leaked key.
options.B: Delete the order-sync service account.
options.C: Search the audit logs for calls made with the leaked key's ID.
options.D: Make the GitHub repository private and keep the key.
options.E: Grant the service account fewer roles and keep the key active.

explanation.summary: A leaked key works for anyone who has a copy until the key is disabled or deleted. Audit log entries record the key ID used to authenticate, so you can see what was done with it.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The key stops working at once, while the VMs keep using the attached account.
option_breakdown.B: Deleting the account breaks order sync, which must keep running.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The logs show whether the key was used, and for what, since it leaked.
option_breakdown.D: Copies already made still work; hiding the repository doesn't revoke the key.
option_breakdown.E: A key that still works is still usable by whoever copied it.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam service-accounts keys disable KEY_ID \
  --iam-account=order-sync@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com

questions.title: A Cloud Run service that reads a secret and publishes events
questions.summary: Grant the service's own service account a narrow role on each resource it uses: Secret Accessor on the secret and Publisher on the topic.
questions.question: The invoicing service at Marsden Co runs on Cloud Run as inv-sa. It must read the current version of one Secret Manager secret, stripe-key, and publish messages to one Pub/Sub topic, invoices. It must do nothing else. Which two grants should you make to inv-sa? (Choose two.)

options.A: Secret Manager Secret Accessor on the stripe-key secret
options.B: Pub/Sub Editor on the whole project
options.C: Editor on the project that hosts the service
options.D: Pub/Sub Publisher on the invoices topic
options.E: Secret Manager Admin on the whole project

explanation.summary: Least privilege means the smallest role, on the smallest resource. Secret Accessor reads secret versions, and Publisher only publishes, each granted on the one resource the service uses.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. It reads stripe-key's payload and nothing else.
option_breakdown.B: Editor on Pub/Sub manages every topic and subscription in the project.
option_breakdown.C: The project Editor role covers almost every service, far beyond the two tasks.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. It can publish to invoices and can't read subscriptions or change topics.
option_breakdown.E: Admin can create, change and delete every secret in the project.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding stripe-key \
  --member=serviceAccount:inv-sa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor
gcloud pubsub topics add-iam-policy-binding invoices \
  --member=serviceAccount:inv-sa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/pubsub.publisher

questions.title: An external auditor who reads policies and audit logs
questions.summary: Security Reviewer reads IAM policies across resources, and Private Logs Viewer reads all logs including Data Access audit logs; neither can change anything.
questions.question: Caldwell Bank hires an outside audit firm for its yearly review. The firm's reviewer needs to inspect who holds which roles on every folder, project and resource, and to read every audit log entry, Data Access entries included. The reviewer must change nothing and see no customer data in buckets or tables. Which two roles should you grant at the organization? (Choose two.)

options.A: Security Reviewer
options.B: Organization Administrator
options.C: Owner
options.D: Viewer

explanation.summary: Security Reviewer lists and reads IAM policies on all resources. Private Logs Viewer reads every log, including Data Access audit logs, which Logs Viewer can't. Both are read-only.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. It reads IAM policies everywhere without being able to change them.
option_breakdown.B: Organization Administrator can change IAM policies across the organization.
option_breakdown.C: Owner can change everything.
option_breakdown.D: The Viewer basic role can read data in many services and doesn't include Data Access audit logs.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. It adds the Data Access audit logs that ordinary log viewing excludes.

questions.title: A service account deleted six weeks ago
questions.summary: A deleted service account can be undeleted only within 30 days; after that, create a new one and grant its roles again.
questions.question: A reporting job at Bramley Press fails because its service account was deleted 45 days ago. Its old role bindings still appear in two projects, prefixed with deleted:. What should you do?

options.A: Undelete the service account by its unique ID.
options.B: Create a service account with the same name; the old bindings apply to it again.
options.C: Create a new service account, grant it the roles, and remove the deleted: bindings.
options.D: Restore the service account from the project's Cloud Asset Inventory history.

explanation.summary: Undelete works for 30 days after deletion. After that the account is gone for good, and its old bindings refer to an identity that no longer exists.

option_breakdown.A: The 30-day undelete window has passed.
option_breakdown.B: A new account with the same name has a new unique ID, and the deleted: bindings don't apply to it.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A new account with fresh grants restores the job, and removing the stale bindings tidies the policies.
option_breakdown.D: Asset history records past metadata; it can't restore a deleted identity.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam service-accounts create report-job --project=P
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding P --member=serviceAccount:report-job@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=ROLE

questions.title: A recreated service account that still gets permission denied
questions.summary: Role bindings point at a service account's unique ID, so a new account with the same email doesn't inherit the deleted account's bindings.
questions.question: Two days after a service account was deleted by mistake at Ferndale Foods, an engineer created a new one with the same name and email. The job using it still gets permission denied, although the project's IAM policy shows the roles granted to that email. What is the best fix?

options.A: Wait an hour for the old bindings to propagate to the new account.
options.B: Delete the new account and undelete the original by its unique ID.
options.C: Disable and re-enable the new service account.
options.D: Grant the roles to the user who runs the job instead.

explanation.summary: The existing bindings belong to the deleted account's unique ID, not to the new account that reuses its email. Within 30 days, undeleting the original brings back the identity those bindings name.

option_breakdown.A: Propagation won't help; the bindings belong to a different identity.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Removing the look-alike frees the email, and undelete restores the original account its bindings refer to.
option_breakdown.C: Disabling and enabling doesn't change which identity the bindings belong to.
option_breakdown.D: Granting roles to a person replaces a workload identity with a human's access, which is the wrong design.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam service-accounts delete report-job@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud iam service-accounts undelete ORIGINAL_UNIQUE_ID

questions.title: Which keys authenticated this month
questions.summary: Cloud Monitoring's service account key metrics record authentication events per key for six weeks, which shows which keys are still in use.
questions.question: Security at Westgate Credit wants to delete every user-managed service account key in a project that hasn't authenticated in the last 30 days. Only generally available tools may be used. Where should you look?

options.A: Cloud Asset Inventory's resource search for service account keys.
options.B: The key authentication metric in Metrics Explorer, grouped by key ID.
options.C: The billing report filtered by service account.
options.D: The VPC Flow Logs of the project's subnets.

explanation.summary: The metric iam.googleapis.com/service_account/key/authn_events_count counts authentications per key and is kept for six weeks, so keys with no data in the last 30 days are unused.

option_breakdown.A: Asset search lists which keys exist, not when they were last used.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Grouping the key authentication metric by key ID shows which keys authenticated in the last 30 days.
option_breakdown.C: Billing doesn't record authentications.
option_breakdown.D: Flow logs show network connections, not which credential a caller used.

explanation.gcloud_command:
# Metrics Explorer: iam.googleapis.com/service_account/key/authn_events_count, group by key_id, last 30 days
gcloud iam service-accounts keys list --iam-account=SA_EMAIL --managed-by=user

questions.title: An HMAC key that belongs to a person
questions.summary: HMAC keys for interoperability should belong to a service account with a role on the specific bucket, not to a user account.
questions.question: For a data migration, a developer at Calder Media created an HMAC key tied to their own user account and configured an S3-compatible tool with it. Security wants the tool's access to be scoped to the target bucket and independent of any person. What should you do?

options.A: Keep the developer's key and remove the developer's other project roles.
options.B: Give the tool a service account JSON key instead of the HMAC key.
options.C: Generate signed URLs for the tool, valid for seven days.
options.D: Create an HMAC key for a service account with a role on the bucket only, and deactivate the user's key.

explanation.summary: An HMAC key acts with the permissions of its owner. A service account that holds only a role on the target bucket keeps the tool's access scoped, and it survives the developer leaving.

option_breakdown.A: The key would still depend on a person's account and that person's remaining access.
option_breakdown.B: An S3-compatible tool can't use a JSON key, and JSON keys are the riskier credential.
option_breakdown.C: Signed URLs cover single objects and expire; they don't give a tool standing access to write a bucket.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A service account HMAC key with a bucket-level role is scoped, revocable and independent of any person.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud storage hmac create migrate-sa@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud storage hmac update ACCESS_ID --deactivated

questions.title: Which endpoint an S3 tool must call
questions.summary: S3-compatible tools use Cloud Storage's XML API at https://storage.googleapis.com with an HMAC key.
questions.question: A backup appliance at Ludlow Clinics has an access ID and secret from a Cloud Storage HMAC key. Its settings ask for an S3 endpoint URL. Which endpoint should you enter?

options.A: https://storage.googleapis.com
options.B: https://s3.amazonaws.com with the bucket's region
options.C: https://www.googleapis.com/storage/v1
options.D: https://console.cloud.google.com/storage

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage's XML API, at storage.googleapis.com, accepts HMAC-signed requests from S3-compatible tools.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The XML API endpoint is the interoperability endpoint that HMAC keys work with.
option_breakdown.B: That endpoint is Amazon S3 itself, which knows nothing of Cloud Storage buckets.
option_breakdown.C: The JSON API uses OAuth tokens, not HMAC signatures.
option_breakdown.D: The console is a web interface for people, not an API endpoint.

explanation.gcloud_command: # S3 tool: endpoint https://storage.googleapis.com, access key = HMAC access ID, secret = HMAC secret

questions.title: A scheduled call to Cloud Run that returns 403
questions.summary: Cloud Run accepts Google-signed ID tokens; a Cloud Scheduler job must send an OIDC token, not an OAuth access token, for a service account with Invoker.
questions.question: A Cloud Scheduler job at Penrith Sport calls a Cloud Run service that requires authentication. The job sends an OAuth token for the service account sched-sa, which has the Cloud Run Invoker role on the service, and every run returns 403. What should you change?

options.A: Grant sched-sa the Editor role on the project.
options.B: Allow unauthenticated invocations on the service.
options.C: Configure the job to send an OIDC token for sched-sa instead.
options.D: Store a key for sched-sa in Secret Manager and send it in a header.

explanation.summary: Cloud Run authenticates callers with Google-signed ID tokens. An OAuth access token is for Google APIs, so Cloud Run rejects it even though the account has Invoker.

option_breakdown.A: The account already has the right role; Editor adds privilege without fixing the token type.
option_breakdown.B: Opening the service to everyone removes the authentication it requires.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An OIDC token with the service's URL as audience is what Cloud Run verifies.
option_breakdown.D: Sending a key in a header isn't an authentication method Cloud Run accepts, and it creates a long-lived secret.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud scheduler jobs update http nightly --location=R \
  --oidc-service-account-email=sched-sa@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com --oidc-token-audience=SERVICE_URL

questions.title: A scheduled job that calls a Google API
questions.summary: Cloud Scheduler sends OAuth access tokens to Google APIs on *.googleapis.com, and OIDC tokens to your own endpoints such as Cloud Run.
questions.question: Every evening a Cloud Scheduler HTTP job at Tilbury Labs must call the Compute Engine API's instances.stop method directly to stop a test VM. The job runs as a service account with the Compute Instance Admin role. How should the job authenticate?

options.A: An OAuth access token for the service account.
options.B: An OIDC token for the service account with the API's URL as audience.
options.C: An API key added to the request's URL.
options.D: No token; Cloud Scheduler's own identity is trusted by Google APIs.

explanation.summary: Google APIs on googleapis.com expect OAuth access tokens. Scheduler mints one for the service account, whose role authorises stopping the VM.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Google APIs are called with OAuth access tokens, which Scheduler creates for the chosen service account.
option_breakdown.B: OIDC tokens are for your own endpoints, such as Cloud Run or Cloud Run functions, not Google APIs.
option_breakdown.C: API keys identify a project, not a principal with IAM roles, and can't authorise stopping a VM.
option_breakdown.D: Scheduler acts as the service account you configure; without a token the call is anonymous and fails.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud scheduler jobs create http stop-test-vm --location=R --schedule='0 19 * * *' --http-method=POST \
  --uri=https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/P/zones/Z/instances/test-vm/stop \
  --oauth-service-account-email=ops-sa@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com

questions.title: Testing a policy change, explaining a denial
questions.summary: Policy Simulator shows the effect of an allow policy change before it is made; Policy Troubleshooter explains one principal's access to one resource.
questions.question: The security team at Ashgrove Mutual has two tasks. Before it removes a broad role binding from a folder, it must test the proposed policy against recent access activity, to learn whether any principal would lose access it actually uses. Separately, it must explain why one developer is denied the permission storage.objects.get on one bucket, taking allow and deny policies into account. Which two tools should the team use? (Choose two.)

options.A: Policy Analyzer
options.B: Role recommendations
options.C: Policy Simulator
options.D: Policy Troubleshooter

explanation.summary: Policy Simulator replays recent access against a proposed allow policy to show what would change. Policy Troubleshooter takes a principal, a resource and a permission and explains how each relevant policy affects that access.

option_breakdown.A: Policy Analyzer lists who has what access under the policies as they are; it neither tests a proposed change nor explains a denial policy by policy.
option_breakdown.B: Role recommendations suggest narrower roles from past usage; they do not simulate this removal or explain one denied request.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Policy Simulator shows how the change might affect principals' access before it is committed.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Policy Troubleshooter examines the allow and deny policies for one principal, resource and permission.
option_breakdown.E: Cloud Asset Inventory records resources and policies and their history; it does not evaluate access.

questions.title: Everyone who can read one sensitive dataset
questions.summary: Policy Analyzer answers which principals have what access to a resource, across inherited policies and groups.
questions.question: An auditor asks Penhallow Bank for the complete list of principals that can read the BigQuery dataset payroll, whether the access was granted on the dataset, on its project, on a folder or on the organization, and whether directly or through a group. Which tool gives the engineer this list?

options.A: The allow policy of the dataset, read with bq show
options.B: Policy Analyzer, with a query for the dataset
options.C: Policy Troubleshooter, with a query for the dataset
options.D: Policy Simulator, with the dataset's current policy

explanation.summary: Policy Analyzer evaluates the allow policies that apply to a resource, including inherited ones, and reports which principals have what access to it.

option_breakdown.A: The dataset's own policy shows only what was granted on the dataset, not what it inherits from the project, folder or organization.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Policy Analyzer finds which principals have what access to a resource, based on all the allow policies.
option_breakdown.C: Policy Troubleshooter checks one named principal and one permission at a time; it does not produce a list of everyone.
option_breakdown.D: Policy Simulator compares a proposed policy with the current one; it does not enumerate who has access today.

questions.title: Developers locked out after the project moved folders
questions.summary: When a project moves, policies inherited from its old parent stop applying, while policies attached to the project itself stay.
questions.question: The project tk-ledger at Tavik Systems was moved from the folder Incubator to the folder Finance. Since the move, the developers, who held Editor through a grant on Incubator, cannot work in the project. A contractor with a grant made directly on tk-ledger still can. The developers need the same access to this project only. What should the administrator do?

options.A: Grant the developers' group Editor on the project tk-ledger
options.B: Grant the developers' group Editor on the folder Finance
options.C: Wait for the Incubator grant to follow the project to its new folder
options.D: Remove the contractor's direct grant, which blocks inherited grants

explanation.summary: A project inherits from wherever it currently sits. After a move, the old parent's inherited policies no longer reach it, and only policies attached directly to the project carry over.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A grant on the project itself restores the developers' access there and applies to nothing else.
option_breakdown.B: A grant on Finance would be inherited by every project in that folder, not only tk-ledger.
option_breakdown.C: Inherited policies do not migrate with a project; the Incubator grant will never apply in Finance.
option_breakdown.D: Allow policies add up. A direct grant never blocks an inherited one, and removing it only locks the contractor out as well.

questions.title: Read access for every employee, present and future
questions.summary: A domain principal stands for all Google Accounts in the Cloud Identity or Workspace domain, so new accounts are covered automatically.
questions.question: Everyone with a Google Account in the Cloud Identity domain of Wickham Press, including people hired later, must be able to read objects in the bucket wp-handbook. Nobody outside the company may read them, and the IT team does not want to maintain a membership list for this. To which principal should Storage Object Viewer on the bucket be granted?

options.A: The domain of Wickham Press
options.B: allAuthenticatedUsers
options.C: allUsers
options.D: A Google group that IT fills with each new employee

explanation.summary: A domain is a virtual group of all the Google Accounts it contains. A new account joins it on creation, so a grant to the domain reaches every employee with no list to keep up.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Every account created in the domain is added to its virtual group, so the grant covers new hires automatically.
option_breakdown.B: This identifier means anyone on the internet signed in with any Google Account, including personal Gmail accounts.
option_breakdown.C: This makes the objects readable by anyone on the internet without signing in at all.
option_breakdown.D: A manually filled group would work only as long as IT keeps the list current, which it wants to avoid.

questions.title: Access that did not expire with its condition
questions.summary: A conditional binding does not limit a principal who also holds the same role without a condition; the unconditional binding must go.
questions.question: A consultant at Rookhope Mining was granted Compute Viewer on the project rm-survey with a condition that expired last Friday. On Monday the consultant can still list the VMs. The project's allow policy contains a second binding of Compute Viewer for the same consultant, added months ago with no condition. What should the administrator do to end the access?

options.A: Remove the expired conditional binding from the project's allow policy
options.B: Add a new Compute Viewer binding for the consultant with the same expiry
options.C: Wait a few more hours for the expiry of the condition to propagate
options.D: Remove the consultant's Compute Viewer binding that has no condition

explanation.summary: Conditional bindings do not override unconditional ones. A principal bound to a role without a condition always has the role, whatever a conditional binding for the same role says.

option_breakdown.A: The expired binding already grants nothing. Removing it tidies the policy but leaves the binding that still grants the role.
option_breakdown.B: Another conditional binding for the same role has no effect while the principal also holds the role without a condition.
option_breakdown.C: The condition took effect on Friday. The access seen on Monday comes from the other binding, so waiting changes nothing.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. While the unconditional binding exists the consultant always has the role, so it has to be removed.

questions.title: An operator for a single VM
questions.summary: Some resources, such as a Compute Engine instance, accept their own allow policy, so a role can be limited to one resource in a project.
questions.question: The project lab-shared at Brandreth College holds forty Compute Engine VMs used by different research groups. A visiting researcher must be able to start, stop and configure the VM gene-seq-01 and must have no rights on the other thirty-nine VMs. Where should Compute Instance Admin (v1) be granted to the researcher?

options.A: On the instance gene-seq-01
options.B: On the project lab-shared
options.C: On the folder that contains lab-shared
options.D: On the persistent disks attached to gene-seq-01

explanation.summary: Allow policies can be set on certain individual resources, including Compute Engine instances. A grant there applies to that resource alone, while a project grant applies to everything in the project.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A role granted on the instance gives the researcher permission on that single VM only.
option_breakdown.B: A project-level grant is inherited by all forty VMs in the project.
option_breakdown.C: A folder-level grant is inherited by every project in the folder and all their VMs.
option_breakdown.D: A grant on the disks covers the disks only; starting, stopping and configuring the VM are permissions on the instance.

questions.title: Read everywhere in the folder, edit in one project
questions.summary: The effective policy is the union of a resource's own policy and what it inherits, so a narrow folder grant plus a broader project grant adds up.
questions.question: A data steward at Yarrow Health needs to view resources in every project of the folder Analytics, including projects added later, and needs to edit resources only in the project ya-catalog, which is in that folder. The fewest possible grants should be used. Which grants meet the requirement?

options.A: Editor on the folder Analytics, and Viewer on every project except ya-catalog
options.B: Viewer on each project of the folder, and Editor on the project ya-catalog
options.C: Editor on the folder Analytics, and a deny policy on each other project
options.D: Viewer on the folder Analytics, and Editor on the project ya-catalog

explanation.summary: Policies inherited from the folder and policies set on the project are combined. Viewer from the folder applies to every project in it, and the project's own Editor grant adds edit rights in that one project.

option_breakdown.A: Editor on the folder is inherited by every project, and a Viewer grant lower down cannot take it away.
option_breakdown.B: Per-project Viewer grants are many grants, and projects added later would have none.
option_breakdown.C: A deny policy per project is many more policies to maintain, and a project added later would inherit Editor with no deny policy.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The effective policy in ya-catalog is the union of the folder's Viewer and the project's Editor.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud resource-manager folders add-iam-policy-binding FOLDER_ID --member="user:steward@example.com" --role="roles/viewer"
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding ya-catalog --member="user:steward@example.com" --role="roles/editor"

questions.title: Federated staff refused by allAuthenticatedUsers
questions.summary: allAuthenticatedUsers covers Google Accounts only, not federated identities; workforce pool users are granted access through the pool's principal set.
questions.question: Staff at Dellmere Housing sign in to Google Cloud through Workforce Identity Federation and have no Google Accounts. To let all staff read a bucket of internal forms, an engineer granted Storage Object Viewer to allAuthenticatedUsers, but staff are still denied. The forms must be readable by staff only. To which principal should the role be granted instead?

options.A: allUsers
options.B: The Cloud Identity domain of Dellmere Housing
options.C: The principal set of the workforce identity pool
options.D: The service agent of Cloud Storage in the project

explanation.summary: allAuthenticatedUsers means principals authenticated with a Google Account. Federated identities are not included, so workforce users are granted roles through a principal set for their pool.

option_breakdown.A: allUsers would let the federated staff in, but also anyone on the internet, and the forms are for staff only.
option_breakdown.B: A domain principal covers the Google Accounts of the domain, and the staff have none.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A principal set for the workforce pool covers the federated staff and nobody else.
option_breakdown.D: A service agent is the identity Google's service uses; granting it a role gives the staff no access.

questions.title: The service agent is missing from the IAM page
questions.summary: The console's IAM page hides service agents until Include Google-provided role grants is selected.
questions.question: A setup guide tells an engineer at Coldharbour Print to grant an additional role to the Compute Engine service agent of the project cp-render. On the project's IAM page in the Google Cloud console the engineer sees users, groups and user-managed service accounts, but no service agent. The Compute Engine API is enabled and VMs are running. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Select Include Google-provided role grants on the IAM page
options.B: Create a service account with the service agent's name
options.C: Disable the Compute Engine API and enable it again
options.D: Look for the service agent on the Service Accounts page

explanation.summary: Service agents are Google-managed service accounts. The IAM page leaves their role grants out of the list unless the Include Google-provided role grants checkbox is selected.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. With the checkbox selected, the page shows service agents and their email addresses, so a role can be added.
option_breakdown.B: A service agent is created and managed by Google; a user-managed account with a similar name is a different principal.
option_breakdown.C: The agent already exists, since VMs are running. Disabling the API would only disrupt them.
option_breakdown.D: The Service Accounts page lists the accounts the project owns; service agents are Google-managed and are not listed there.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > IAM & Admin > IAM > Include Google-provided role grants

questions.title: A project Owner cannot create a deny policy
questions.summary: Creating and managing deny policies requires the Deny Admin role; project ownership does not include it.
questions.question: A security engineer at Ivybridge Water is Owner of the project iw-scada and wants to attach a deny policy to it, so that nobody can delete its Cloud Storage buckets. The attempt to create the deny policy fails with a permission error. Which role does the engineer need?

options.A: Project IAM Admin
options.B: Organization Policy Administrator
options.C: Deny Admin
options.D: Storage Admin

explanation.summary: Deny policies have their own permissions. Viewing them takes Deny Reviewer, and creating, updating or deleting them takes Deny Admin; the Owner role does not carry these permissions.

option_breakdown.A: Project IAM Admin administers the project's allow policy; deny policies are managed with different permissions.
option_breakdown.B: This role manages organization policy constraints, which are a separate kind of policy from IAM deny policies.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Deny Admin, granted on the organization, is the role for viewing, creating, updating and deleting deny policies.
option_breakdown.D: Storage Admin manages buckets and objects; it gives no permission to write an IAM deny policy.

questions.title: A role on the IAM page that cannot be edited
questions.summary: An inherited role is shown on a child's IAM page but can be changed only on the resource where it was granted.
questions.question: On the IAM page of the project vx-billing at Voxley Group, an administrator sees that the group interns has the Editor role, marked as inherited from the folder Shared. The administrator, who is Owner of the project and Folder Admin on Shared, wants to change that grant, but the project's IAM page does not allow editing it. Where should the change be made?

options.A: On the project, by adding a Viewer grant for interns that overrides Editor
options.B: On the folder Shared, where the role was granted
options.C: On the organization, where all inherited roles are stored
options.D: On the project, with gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding

explanation.summary: The console lists inherited grants on a resource's IAM page for visibility, but an inherited role belongs to the policy of the ancestor that granted it and is edited there.

option_breakdown.A: Allow policies are additive. A Viewer grant on the project adds to the inherited Editor and overrides nothing.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Inherited roles are edited on the resource where the role was granted, here the folder.
option_breakdown.C: The grant is in the folder's allow policy; the organization's policy does not contain it.
option_breakdown.D: The binding is not in the project's allow policy, so there is nothing for the project-level command to remove.

questions.title: An Owner who cannot delete a service account key
questions.summary: A deny policy on a resource or an ancestor is checked before allow policies, so it blocks a permission whatever roles the principal holds.
questions.question: An engineer at Quarrington Rail holds the Owner role on the project qr-signals, granted directly on the project. When the engineer tries to delete a service account key in that project, the request is refused for lack of the permission, although Owner contains it. The organization uses IAM deny policies. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The Owner role takes up to 24 hours to become effective on a project
options.B: An allow policy on the folder grants the engineer only the Viewer role
options.C: A deny policy on the project or one of its ancestors denies that permission
options.D: The service account key was created by another user, who must delete it

explanation.summary: IAM checks relevant deny policies before allow policies. A denied permission cannot be used regardless of granted roles, and deny policies are inherited from the organization and folders.

option_breakdown.A: Role grants propagate in minutes, and nothing in the scenario suggests the grant is new.
option_breakdown.B: Allow policies add up, so a smaller role higher in the hierarchy cannot reduce what Owner on the project grants.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A denied permission cannot be used whatever roles the principal has, and deny policies are inherited.
option_breakdown.D: Deleting a key depends on the permission, not on who created the key.

questions.title: A custom role deleted two days ago
questions.summary: A deleted custom role can be undeleted within 7 days; its bindings stay in the policies and take effect again.
questions.question: Two days ago, during a clean-up, the custom role logReaderLite was deleted from the project ek-data at Eskdale Mills. The thirty analysts bound to it now get permission errors, although their bindings still appear in the project's allow policy. A deleted custom role can be undeleted for 7 days. Access must return exactly as it was. What should the administrator do?

options.A: Create a new custom role with the ID logReaderLite and the same permissions
options.B: Add the thirty analysts' bindings to the allow policy again
options.C: Undelete the custom role logReaderLite in the project
options.D: Grant the analysts the Editor role until the role is rebuilt

explanation.summary: When a custom role is deleted, bindings that refer to it stay in the allow policy without effect. Undeleting the role within 7 days returns it to its previous state and the bindings work again.

option_breakdown.A: While the deleted role is still within its 7 days, its role ID is not free to be used for a new role.
option_breakdown.B: The bindings are still in the policy; they have no effect because the role they name is deleted.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Undeleting returns the role to its previous state, and the existing bindings take effect again.
option_breakdown.D: Editor is far broader than a log-reading role and is not the access the analysts had.

questions.title: Switching a custom role off during an investigation
questions.summary: A custom role set to the DISABLED launch stage stays in every policy but grants nothing, and can be enabled again.
questions.question: The custom role dataFixer at Morland Seeds is bound to principals in fourteen projects. Security suspects it contains a dangerous permission and wants it to stop granting any access today while the role is reviewed. If the review clears it, access must come back without anyone re-creating the fourteen sets of bindings. What should the administrator do?

options.A: Delete the role and create it again after the review
options.B: Remove the role's bindings from the fourteen projects
options.C: Change the role's launch stage to DEPRECATED
options.D: Change the role's launch stage to DISABLED

explanation.summary: A disabled custom role still appears in allow policies but has no effect. Changing the stage back restores its effect, with every binding still in place.

option_breakdown.A: A role created afresh after the review is a new role; nothing in the scenario allows for the risk and delay of deleting it first.
option_breakdown.B: Removing the bindings stops the access, but all fourteen sets would have to be re-created afterwards.
option_breakdown.C: DEPRECATED is informational: it marks a role as no longer in use but the role keeps granting its permissions.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A disabled role stays in the policies but grants nothing, and it can be enabled again later.

questions.title: A new feature that custom-role users cannot use
questions.summary: Google updates predefined roles when features need new permissions; a custom role gets them only when its owner adds them.
questions.question: A year ago Lindqvist Dairy built the custom role storageOperator from the permissions of a predefined Cloud Storage role. Google has since released a storage feature that needs one additional permission. Colleagues who hold the predefined role can use the feature; holders of storageOperator get a permission error. The custom role should stay as narrow as it is. What should the administrator do?

options.A: Wait for Google to add the new permission to storageOperator
options.B: Replace storageOperator with the Editor role for its holders
options.C: Add the new permission to the custom role storageOperator
options.D: Delete storageOperator and undelete it to refresh its permissions

explanation.summary: Predefined roles are maintained by Google and gain permissions as services evolve. Custom roles are maintained by their owner, who must add the permissions that new features require.

option_breakdown.A: Google maintains predefined roles only. A custom role never receives a permission unless its owner adds it.
option_breakdown.B: Editor would unlock the feature but grants change rights across almost every service, the opposite of a narrow role.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The owner of a custom role updates it to let users access features that need additional permissions.
option_breakdown.D: Undeleting returns a role to its previous state; it does not pull in permissions from the predefined role.

questions.title: Who may define custom roles in one project
questions.summary: Role Administrator on a project lets a principal create and manage that project's custom roles and nothing else.
questions.question: An IAM specialist at Padbury Tools must create, update and delete custom roles in the project pt-factory. The specialist must not be able to grant roles to anyone, must not manage custom roles of the organization, and must not change other resources in the project. Which grant fits?

options.A: Project IAM Admin on the project pt-factory
options.B: Organization Role Administrator on the organization
options.C: Role Administrator on the project pt-factory
options.D: Service Account Admin on the project pt-factory

explanation.summary: Managing custom roles is its own job with its own role: Role Administrator for a project's roles, Organization Role Administrator for an organization's.

option_breakdown.A: Project IAM Admin edits the allow policy, that is, who holds which role; it does not define roles and it allows granting.
option_breakdown.B: This role manages the organization's custom roles, which the specialist must not do.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Role Administrator on the project is the role for managing that project's custom roles.
option_breakdown.D: Service Account Admin manages service accounts, which are identities, not role definitions.

questions.title: A permission a project-level custom role refuses
questions.summary: A permission that works only at the organization or folder level cannot go into a project-level custom role; the role must be an organization-level one.
questions.question: An engineer at Stanmore Glass is creating the custom role platformReader in the project sg-tools. The role's permission list includes resourcemanager.organizations.get, and creating the role fails with an error about that permission. The role's holders do need to read the organization's details. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Create the role in a different project that has more APIs enabled
options.B: Create the role as a custom role of the organization
options.C: Set the role's launch stage to ALPHA and create it again
options.D: Grant the Owner role on sg-tools in place of the custom role

explanation.summary: A project-level custom role may contain any supported permission except those that can be used only at the organization or folder level. Such permissions belong in an organization-level custom role.

option_breakdown.A: Any project-level custom role rejects this permission; the project and its enabled APIs make no difference.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A permission usable only at organization level cannot be in a project-level role, so the role is created at the organization.
option_breakdown.C: The launch stage is a label for the role's maturity and has no effect on which permissions it may contain.
option_breakdown.D: Owner on a project gives sweeping rights in the project and still no right to read the organization's details.

questions.title: What exactly does this predefined role contain
questions.summary: A role's metadata, read with gcloud iam roles describe, lists every permission the role contains.
questions.question: Before granting the predefined role roles/cloudsql.editor to a contractor, a reviewer at Ansty Motors must confirm whether the role includes the permission to delete Cloud SQL instances. Nobody holds the role yet, so there is no existing access to examine. How should the reviewer find out?

options.A: Read the project's allow policy with gcloud projects get-iam-policy
options.B: Run Policy Troubleshooter for the contractor and a Cloud SQL instance
options.C: Look at the role recommendations for the project
options.D: Read the role's permissions with gcloud iam roles describe

explanation.summary: Every role has metadata that includes its list of permissions. Describing the role shows that list without anyone having to hold the role.

option_breakdown.A: An allow policy shows which principals hold which roles, not which permissions a role is made of.
option_breakdown.B: Policy Troubleshooter evaluates access a principal currently has; the contractor has not been granted the role yet.
option_breakdown.C: Recommendations are built from how granted roles were used, and this role has not been granted to anyone.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Describing the role returns its metadata, including the permissions it contains.

questions.title: A permission that custom roles do not support
questions.summary: A permission with the support level NOT_SUPPORTED cannot be put in a custom role; it is obtained through a predefined role.
questions.question: Corvedale Signs is assembling a custom role for its operators. One permission the operators need is listed with the custom-role support level NOT_SUPPORTED. The other fifteen permissions are supported and are already in the custom role. The operators must end up with all sixteen permissions and as little beyond them as possible. What should the administrator do?

options.A: Add the permission to the custom role and set the stage to BETA
options.B: Also grant the narrowest predefined role that contains the permission
options.C: Create the custom role at the organization level, where it is supported
options.D: Grant the operators the Owner role, which contains every permission

explanation.summary: Each permission has a support level for custom roles. One that is not supported cannot be included in any custom role, so it has to come from a predefined role granted alongside.

option_breakdown.A: The launch stage of a role does not change which permissions custom roles are allowed to contain.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The permission is not supported in custom roles, so a narrow predefined role supplies it next to the custom role.
option_breakdown.C: The support level belongs to the permission, not to where the role is created, so an organization-level role rejects it too.
option_breakdown.D: Owner supplies the permission, along with almost every other permission in the project, far beyond the sixteen needed.

questions.title: Marking a custom role as on its way out
questions.summary: Launch stages other than DISABLED are informational: DEPRECATED tells administrators a role is no longer in use without changing what it grants.
questions.question: Elmstead Foods is replacing its custom role legacyDeployer with two narrower roles over the next quarter. Until the migration ends, current holders of legacyDeployer must keep exactly the access they have. Meanwhile, anyone who looks at the role should see that it is no longer meant to be used. What should the administrator do with legacyDeployer now?

options.A: Change its launch stage to DISABLED
options.B: Delete it, and undelete it if a holder complains
options.C: Change its launch stage to DEPRECATED
options.D: Remove all of its permissions and keep the bindings

explanation.summary: A custom role's launch stage is metadata. Stages such as ALPHA, BETA, GA and DEPRECATED are informational and do not change the role's effect; only DISABLED turns the role off.

option_breakdown.A: A disabled role stops granting anything at once, which cuts off the current holders before the migration.
option_breakdown.B: A deleted role's bindings stop working immediately, so holders would lose access until someone undeletes it.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. DEPRECATED signals that the role is no longer in use, while its permissions keep working.
option_breakdown.D: A role with no permissions grants nothing, so the holders would lose their access at once.

questions.title: A service agent created ahead of time does nothing
questions.summary: A service agent created at a user's request is not granted its usual roles automatically; they must be granted by hand.
questions.question: To prepare a new project, an engineer at Brightwell Paper asked Google Cloud to create the service agent of a service before the service was first used, and the command returned the agent's email address. When the team later starts using the service, it fails because its service agent lacks permissions in the project. In older projects, where the agent appeared on first use, the service works. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Delete the service agent so that Google Cloud creates it again on next use
options.B: Create a user-managed service account with the same email address
options.C: Grant the service agent the role it is normally granted automatically
options.D: Disable the service's API and enable it again in the new project

explanation.summary: Service agents that appear on first use are usually granted their service agent role automatically. An agent created on request is not, so the role has to be granted manually.

option_breakdown.A: Service agents are managed by Google and are not in the project's list of service accounts, so they cannot be deleted from there.
option_breakdown.B: A service agent's address is in a Google-owned domain; a user-managed account cannot take it and would not be used by the service.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An agent created at a user's request gets no roles automatically, so its usual role must be granted.
option_breakdown.D: The agent already exists, so enabling the API again creates nothing new and grants nothing.

questions.title: An unknown account changed the project's allow policy
questions.summary: service-agent-manager@system.gserviceaccount.com is Google's role manager for service agents; its policy changes when a new API is used are expected.
questions.question: Reviewing Admin Activity audit logs, a security analyst at Farleigh Marine finds that the principal service-agent-manager@system.gserviceaccount.com set the allow policy of the project fm-ops yesterday. Nobody in the company recognises the account. The change added a role whose name ends in serviceAgent to a Google-managed account, shortly after a team enabled a new API. What should the analyst conclude?

options.A: A key of a user-managed service account has leaked and must be rotated
options.B: A project Owner impersonated a service account to hide the change
options.C: A default service account was created and granted the Editor role
options.D: Google Cloud granted a new service agent its role, which is expected

explanation.summary: When a new API is used, Google Cloud may create a service agent and grant it roles. The grant is made by the role manager for service agents, an account that is visible only in audit logs.

option_breakdown.A: The account is in the Google-owned system domain, not a user-managed account in a project, and it has no user-held keys.
option_breakdown.B: Impersonation is logged with the impersonated account and the caller; it would not appear as this Google system account.
option_breakdown.C: The role added ends in serviceAgent and went to a Google-managed account; a default service account and Editor are not involved.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. This account manages the roles granted to service agents, and such entries follow first use of an API.

questions.title: No more service accounts can be created
questions.summary: The number of service accounts in a project is a quota, Service Account Count, which can be viewed and raised like other quotas.
questions.question: The project hv-micro at Havering Tech runs one user-managed service account per microservice, as company policy requires, and every existing account is in use. Creating the account for a new microservice fails because the project has reached its limit of service accounts. Policy also says a workload's service account must live in the workload's own project. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Create the account in another project and grant it roles in hv-micro
options.B: Request a higher Service Account Count quota for hv-micro
options.C: Let the new microservice share the account of an existing one
options.D: Run the new microservice as the Compute Engine default service account

explanation.summary: How many service accounts a project may hold is set by the Service Account Count quota, which appears among the project's quotas and can be increased on request.

option_breakdown.A: An account in another project would work technically but breaks the rule that it lives in the workload's project.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The limit is a project quota named Service Account Count, so the fix is a quota increase.
option_breakdown.C: Sharing an account breaks the rule of one account per microservice and merges the two services' permissions.
option_breakdown.D: The default account is shared by anything that does not specify one, so this also breaks the one-per-service rule.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > IAM & Admin > Quotas & System Limits > filter: Service Account Count > Edit

questions.title: Taking Editor away from the default service account
questions.summary: A default service account that holds Editor is narrowed by finding what it uses and replacing Editor with less permissive roles.
questions.question: In the three-year-old project om-store at Oakmere Retail, the Compute Engine default service account holds the Editor role, and a dozen VMs run as that account. Security wants the account reduced to what the VMs really need, without breaking them. Which two actions should the engineer take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Delete the default service account so that Google Cloud re-creates it
options.B: Use role recommendations to see which permissions the account uses
options.C: Disable the default service account until the review is finished
options.D: Grant it the narrower roles it needs, then revoke the Editor role
options.E: Create a key for the account and move the VMs to key-based access

explanation.summary: The recommendation for a default service account with Editor is to replace Editor with less permissive roles. Role recommendations show what an older binding really uses, so the replacement can be made safely.

option_breakdown.A: Deleting the account breaks every VM that runs as it, and a default account is not simply re-created with the right roles.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. For a binding older than 90 days, role recommendations show which roles to grant instead.
option_breakdown.C: A disabled account cannot authenticate, so all twelve VMs would lose access during the review.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Granting the needed roles first and revoking Editor afterwards narrows the account without an outage.
option_breakdown.E: A key is a long-lived credential that adds risk and does nothing to reduce the account's permissions.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud recommender recommendations list --project=om-store --location=global --recommender=google.iam.policy.Recommender
gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding om-store --member="serviceAccount:PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com" --role="roles/editor"

questions.title: A deny rule for everyone that broke Google's services
questions.summary: A deny rule that targets all principals should list the service agents as exceptions, or Google Cloud services stop working.
questions.question: Tolworth Labs attached a deny policy to its organization that denies several storage permissions to the principal set of all principals, with only the storage administrators' group as an exception. Soon afterwards Google Cloud services that write to the company's buckets on its behalf began to fail. The deny rule must stay in force for people and for the company's own service accounts. What should be changed?

options.A: Grant the Storage Admin role to every affected service agent
options.B: Move the deny policy from the organization to each project
options.C: Replace the deny policy with an allow policy condition
options.D: Add the organization's service agents as exception principals

explanation.summary: A principal set of all principals includes service agents. Deny rules win over any granted role, so the recommended practice is to list the service agents as exceptions in such a rule.

option_breakdown.A: A deny rule is checked before allow policies, so no additional role lets the agents use a denied permission.
option_breakdown.B: At project level the same rule would still cover the service agents that act in those projects.
option_breakdown.C: The rule must stay in force, and allow policy conditions cannot take away a permission granted elsewhere.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Listing the service agents as exceptions keeps the rule for everyone else and lets the services work.

questions.title: A script that wants to run as a service agent
questions.summary: Service agents are Google-managed and cannot be used directly; a workload of your own needs a user-managed service account.
questions.question: A developer at Wendover Print notices that a Google Cloud service's service agent already has the access to a bucket that a new nightly script of the developer's also needs. To save time, the developer wants the script to authenticate as that service agent. The service agent does not appear in the project's list of service accounts. What should the developer do?

options.A: Create a user-managed service account for the script and grant it the access
options.B: Create a key for the service agent and give the key file to the script
options.C: Select Include Google-provided role grants and attach the agent to the script's VM
options.D: Grant the developer Service Account User on the service agent and impersonate it

explanation.summary: Service agents are created and managed by Google for its own services. They are not in your project and cannot be accessed directly, so your own workloads use service accounts that you create.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A user-managed service account is the identity you create and control for your own workload.
option_breakdown.B: Service agents are not in the project and cannot be accessed directly, so no key can be created for one.
option_breakdown.C: The checkbox only shows the agent's role grants on the IAM page; it does not make the agent attachable to a VM.
option_breakdown.D: A service agent is not a resource in the project on which the developer could be granted a role.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud iam service-accounts create nightly-script --display-name="Nightly script"

questions.title: A VM that may read one bucket and no other
questions.summary: Access scopes are coarse and cannot single out a bucket; a dedicated service account with a role on that bucket can.
questions.question: A VM at Ullswater Maps runs a job that must read objects from the bucket um-tiles and from no other bucket in the project. The VM currently runs as the Compute Engine default service account, which can read every bucket. An engineer suggests keeping that account and setting the VM's access scope to read-only storage. What should be done to meet the requirement?

options.A: Keep the default account and set the access scope to devstorage.read_only
options.B: Keep the default account and set the access scope to cloud-platform
options.C: Attach a dedicated service account with Storage Object Viewer on um-tiles
options.D: Attach a dedicated service account with Storage Object Viewer on the whole project

explanation.summary: Access scopes restrict a VM by service and kind of operation, not by resource. Limiting a workload to one bucket takes an allow policy on that bucket for a service account of its own.

option_breakdown.A: A read-only storage scope limits the VM to read operations in Cloud Storage but still across every bucket the account can read.
option_breakdown.B: The cloud-platform scope removes scope restrictions altogether, leaving the default account's access to all buckets.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A dedicated account with a role on the single bucket restricts the VM to exactly that bucket.
option_breakdown.D: A role on the project lets the dedicated account read objects in every bucket of the project.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://um-tiles --member="serviceAccount:tiles-job@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com" --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
gcloud compute instances set-service-account VM_NAME --zone=ZONE --service-account=tiles-job@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com --scopes=cloud-platform

questions.title: The constraint is on, yet Editor is still there
questions.summary: Enforcing the automatic-grants constraint stops future Editor grants to default service accounts but leaves existing grants in place.
questions.question: Last month Whitmore Glass enforced the organization policy constraint that disables automatic IAM grants for default service accounts. An audit this week shows that the Compute Engine default service accounts in the company's forty older projects still hold the Editor role. The auditor asks why, and what will fix it. What should the engineer answer?

options.A: The constraint needs more time to propagate, so the roles will disappear by themselves
options.B: The constraint does not remove existing grants, so Editor must be removed in those projects
options.C: The constraint works only on folders, so it must be set again on each folder
options.D: The constraint applies to service agents, so a different constraint is needed

explanation.summary: The constraint prevents the automatic Editor grant when a default service account is created. It does not go back and remove the role from accounts that already have it.

option_breakdown.A: Propagation is not the issue: the constraint never removes a role that was granted before it was enforced.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Existing default service accounts keep Editor until someone replaces it with narrower roles.
option_breakdown.C: The constraint can be set on the organization, a folder or a project and is inherited downwards.
option_breakdown.D: The constraint is about default service accounts, which is exactly what the audit found.

questions.title: A new project where the default account can do nothing
questions.summary: With automatic grants disabled, a default service account in a new project has no access; a workload needs an account with the roles it uses.
questions.question: Rushmere Pumps enforces the constraint that disables automatic IAM grants for default service accounts. In a project created yesterday, a VM was started without specifying a service account, and its job fails with permission errors when it writes to a Pub/Sub topic in the same project. In older projects the same job works. Following least privilege, what should the engineer do?

options.A: Grant the Editor role to the project's Compute Engine default service account
options.B: Remove the organization policy constraint for the new project
