options.C: Set the VM's access scope to cloud-platform and restart the job
options.D: Run the VM as a dedicated service account with Publisher on the topic

explanation.summary: Under the constraint, the default service account of a new project starts with no roles. The workload should run as its own service account holding only the role it needs.

option_breakdown.A: Editor would make the job work by recreating the over-broad grant the constraint exists to prevent.
option_breakdown.B: Lifting the constraint would not grant anything to the account that already exists, and it weakens the control.
option_breakdown.C: Scopes only restrict what granted roles allow; the account has no roles, so no scope can make the job work.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A dedicated account with Publisher on that one topic gives the job exactly the access it needs.

questions.title: What to check before Editor is taken away
questions.summary: Google's services act through service agents, not default service accounts, so removing Editor from a default account affects only the workloads that run as it.
questions.question: A team at Carleton Dairy wants to remove the Editor role from the Compute Engine default service account of its project. A colleague objects that Google Cloud's own services in the project, such as managed instance groups and log sinks, will stop working because they depend on that role. What should the team check before removing the role?

options.A: Which of its own VMs and jobs run as the default account, and what they access
options.B: Which Google Cloud services are enabled in the project, since each needs the role
options.C: Whether the project's service agents hold the Editor role as well
options.D: Whether the default account has user-managed keys that would be deleted

explanation.summary: The Editor grant on a default service account is a convenience, not something Google's services need: they reach resources through service agents. Only workloads that run as the default account rely on its roles.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The team's own workloads that run as the account are what the change can break, so they are what to check.
option_breakdown.B: Google Cloud services use service agents to access resources, so enabled services do not depend on this role.
option_breakdown.C: Service agents have their own service agent roles; whether they hold Editor has no bearing on the default account.
option_breakdown.D: Removing a role from an account does not delete or affect any of the account's keys.

questions.title: Junior admins on a VM with a powerful account
questions.summary: Anyone who can run code on a resource can act with its attached service account, so the attached account must hold only what the resource needs.
questions.question: At Stokesay Rail the VM batch-01 runs as a service account that holds Owner on the project, a leftover from a prototype. Its job only reads one Cloud Storage bucket. Junior administrators can SSH to batch-01 with keys kept in its metadata and run commands on it, but hold no role on any service account. Security wants to stop them from being able to act with Owner rights. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Remove the Service Account Token Creator role from the junior administrators
options.B: Rotate the keys of the service account that is attached to batch-01
options.C: Move batch-01 to a subnet without an external IP address
options.D: Give batch-01 a service account that can only read that bucket

explanation.summary: Code running on a VM obtains tokens for the attached service account from the metadata server. Users who can run code there gain the account's permissions without any impersonation role.

option_breakdown.A: They hold no such role. They act through the VM's attached account, not through impersonation.
option_breakdown.B: The VM gets its tokens from the metadata server, not from keys, so rotating keys changes nothing for people on the VM.
option_breakdown.C: Where the VM sits in the network does not change which permissions its attached account has.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. With a least-privileged account attached, running code on the VM yields only read access to the bucket.

questions.title: Handing an access token to another component
questions.summary: A Credential Access Boundary downscopes an access token so that a component it is passed to can reach only the Cloud Storage resources it needs.
questions.question: A backend at Pennard Media runs as a service account that can read and write twenty Cloud Storage buckets. For each upload it passes an access token to a third-party conversion component, which needs to read objects in the bucket pm-raw only; that bucket uses uniform bucket-level access. Tokens are bearer tokens, so the component could use a full token on all twenty buckets. What should the backend do?

options.A: Pass the token it has, and remove the component's network access to other buckets
options.B: Pass a token downscoped with a Credential Access Boundary to reading pm-raw
options.C: Pass a service account key, so that the component can create its own tokens
options.D: Pass an ID token for the service account in place of the access token

explanation.summary: An access token carries all the access of the account it was issued for. Downscoping with a Credential Access Boundary yields a token limited to chosen Cloud Storage resources and permissions.

option_breakdown.A: Buckets are reached through the same Google APIs endpoint, so network rules cannot separate one bucket from another.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A downscoped token grants enough access to pm-raw and no more, whoever ends up holding it.
option_breakdown.C: A key is a long-lived credential for the whole account, far more than the component should hold.
option_breakdown.D: An ID token proves identity to a service; it does not authorize calls to the Cloud Storage API.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Security Token Service: exchange the access token with a Credential Access Boundary that allows roles/storage.objectViewer on pm-raw

questions.title: Service accounts that can hop between projects
questions.summary: Recommender's lateral movement insights find roles that let a service account in one project impersonate one in another.
questions.question: After a penetration test, Evenwood Bank learns that an attacker who controlled one service account could have impersonated a service account in a second project, and from there one in a third. The security team wants a list of the role grants across the organization that allow a service account in one project to impersonate a service account in another. Which tool provides it?

options.A: VPC Flow Logs for the projects' networks
options.B: Policy Simulator for each project's allow policy
options.C: The key authentication metrics in Cloud Monitoring
options.D: Lateral movement insights in Recommender

explanation.summary: Lateral movement is a service account in one project being able to impersonate one in another. Recommender produces insights that identify the roles allowing it, some with recommendations to remove them.

option_breakdown.A: Flow logs record network traffic between addresses; impersonation is an IAM permission, not a network flow.
option_breakdown.B: Policy Simulator tests a proposed policy change; it does not search for cross-project impersonation grants.
option_breakdown.C: Key metrics show which service account keys were used; they say nothing about who may impersonate whom.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. These insights identify roles that let a service account in one project impersonate one in another.

questions.title: A deployer who may attach one service account
questions.summary: Roles on service accounts are granted on the individual account; a project-level grant covers every service account in the project.
questions.question: The project rb-apps at Rosebank Media holds thirty service accounts, several with powerful roles. A developer deploys VMs for the web team and must be able to attach the service account web-frontend to them, and no other service account. Where should the Service Account User role be granted to the developer?

options.A: On the project rb-apps
options.B: On the folder that contains rb-apps
options.C: On the service account web-frontend
options.D: On each VM that the developer deploys

explanation.summary: A service account is a resource with its own allow policy. Service Account User granted there covers that account alone, while the same role on a project applies to every service account in it.

option_breakdown.A: A project-level grant would let the developer attach any of the thirty accounts, including the powerful ones.
option_breakdown.B: A folder-level grant reaches every service account in every project of the folder, which is wider still.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Access to service accounts is managed for each account individually, so the grant goes on web-frontend.
option_breakdown.D: The role concerns the service account, not the VM; a grant on a VM does not allow attaching an account to it.

questions.title: A central service account that will not attach
questions.summary: Attaching a service account from another project also requires the resource project's service agent to hold Token Creator on that account.
questions.question: Garsdale Tools keeps all its service accounts in the project gt-identities. An engineer creates a Compute Engine VM in the project gt-orders and tries to attach orders-vm, a service account from gt-identities. The engineer has Service Account User on orders-vm, and the organization policy that blocks cross-project use is not enforced on gt-identities. The attachment still fails. What is missing?

options.A: The Owner role for the engineer on the project gt-identities
options.B: A user-managed key for orders-vm, stored on the new VM
options.C: Token Creator on orders-vm for the Compute Engine service agent of gt-orders
options.D: A VPC Network Peering connection between the networks of the two projects

explanation.summary: For a cross-project attachment, the service that owns the resource obtains tokens for the account through its service agent. That agent must be granted Service Account Token Creator on the service account.

option_breakdown.A: The engineer already has the role needed to attach the account; what lacks access is the service, not the person.
option_breakdown.B: An attached account is served tokens by the metadata server; a key on the VM is unnecessary and adds risk.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The service agent of the resource's service needs Token Creator on the account to act as it.
option_breakdown.D: Attaching a service account is an IAM matter; it does not depend on network connectivity between projects.

questions.title: Moving a running VM off the default account
questions.summary: A VM's service account can be changed only while the VM is stopped.
questions.question: The VM report-01 at Skelton Energy has run for a year as the Compute Engine default service account. A dedicated service account, report-sa, now exists with the roles the VM's job needs. The engineer must switch report-01 to report-sa and keep the VM, its disks and its internal IP address. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Edit the running VM and select report-sa as its service account
options.B: Stop the VM, set report-sa as its service account, and start it
options.C: Delete the VM and create it again from a snapshot with report-sa
options.D: Create a key for report-sa and copy the key file onto the VM

explanation.summary: The attached service account and access scopes are properties that can be changed only on a stopped VM. After the change the same VM is started again.

option_breakdown.A: The service account of a running VM cannot be edited; the VM has to be stopped first.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. To change a VM's service account you must first stop the VM, then restart it afterwards.
option_breakdown.C: Recreating the VM is unnecessary work and puts at risk the things that must be kept.
option_breakdown.D: The VM would still run as the default account, and a key file on disk is a long-lived credential to protect.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances stop report-01 --zone=ZONE
gcloud compute instances set-service-account report-01 --zone=ZONE --service-account=report-sa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com --scopes=cloud-platform
gcloud compute instances start report-01 --zone=ZONE

questions.title: A job in one project reading a bucket in another
questions.summary: A service account is a principal that can be granted a role on a resource in any project; no second account is needed.
questions.question: A Cloud Run job in the project hn-etl at Hawnby Analytics runs as the service account etl-job, which belongs to hn-etl. The job must read objects in the bucket hn-landing, which belongs to the project hn-lake. It needs nothing else in hn-lake. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Grant etl-job Storage Object Viewer on the bucket hn-landing
options.B: Create a second service account in hn-lake and give its key to the job
options.C: Grant etl-job Storage Object Viewer on the project hn-etl
options.D: Move the bucket hn-landing into the project hn-etl

explanation.summary: As a principal, a service account can be named in the allow policy of any resource, whichever project owns that resource. The narrowest grant is on the one bucket.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The account is granted the read role on that bucket in the other project, and nothing more.
option_breakdown.B: A second account and a key add a long-lived credential for something the job's own identity can be granted.
option_breakdown.C: A role on hn-etl covers buckets of hn-etl; the bucket to be read belongs to hn-lake.
option_breakdown.D: A bucket cannot be moved between projects, and the data's ownership should not change to satisfy one reader.

questions.title: Getting rid of an unused default service account
questions.summary: A deleted default service account cannot be recreated, so one that might be needed later is left disabled.
questions.question: All workloads in the project ts-core at Thirlby Systems now run as dedicated service accounts. The security team wants the Compute Engine default service account, which nothing uses any more, made unusable. The platform team says a product they may adopt next year could need the default account. What should the engineer do with the default service account?

options.A: Disable it and leave it in the project
options.B: Delete it and recreate it if it is needed
options.C: Create a key for it and store the key offline
options.D: Grant it the Viewer role in place of Editor

explanation.summary: A disabled service account cannot authenticate, and it can be enabled again with its bindings intact. A default service account, once deleted, cannot be recreated.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Disabled, the account is unusable now and can be enabled later if the product needs it.
option_breakdown.B: Default service accounts cannot be recreated after they are deleted, so this closes the door on next year's product.
option_breakdown.C: A key is a new way to use the account, the opposite of making it unusable.
option_breakdown.D: With Viewer the account can still authenticate and read every resource in the project.

questions.title: No service account keys in the production folder
questions.summary: The organization policy constraints that disable key creation and key upload stop everyone from making service account keys, whatever roles they hold.
questions.question: No workload in the folder Production at Wetherby Health needs service account keys: everything runs on attached service accounts. Security wants to make sure that nobody, including project Owners, can create or upload a service account key in any project of that folder, now or in projects added later. What should be done?

options.A: Remove the Service Account Key Admin role from every user in the folder
options.B: Enforce the constraints that disable key creation and key upload on the folder
options.C: Set a key rotation reminder of 90 days for every service account
options.D: Disable every user-managed service account in the folder's projects

explanation.summary: The two organization policy constraints block key creation and key upload for all users, even those whose roles include the permission, and a policy on a folder is inherited by its projects.

option_breakdown.A: Owners and other broad roles also contain the key permissions, so removing one role leaves the door open.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The constraints prevent all users from creating and uploading keys, including those with the permission.
option_breakdown.C: Rotation manages keys that exist; the aim is that no keys can be created at all.
option_breakdown.D: Disabled accounts would stop the workloads that run as them, and keys could still be created for an enabled one.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud resource-manager org-policies enable-enforce iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation --folder=FOLDER_ID
gcloud resource-manager org-policies enable-enforce iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload --folder=FOLDER_ID

questions.title: The proxy connects, the IAM database login is refused
questions.summary: With IAM database authentication, a service account needs Cloud SQL Instance User in addition to Cloud SQL Client.
questions.question: A reporting job at Seathwaite Farms runs as the service account report-job, which holds Cloud SQL Client on the project. The job reaches its Cloud SQL instance through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy without trouble. The team has now switched the job from a database password to IAM database authentication and added report-job as an IAM database user on the instance, but the database login as report-job is refused. Following least privilege, which role must report-job be granted in addition?

options.A: Cloud SQL Admin
options.B: Cloud SQL Instance User
options.C: Service Account Token Creator
options.D: Cloud SQL Viewer

explanation.summary: Connecting through the proxy needs Cloud SQL Client. Logging in to the database as an IAM principal is a second permission, carried by Cloud SQL Instance User.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud SQL Admin would cover the login, along with full control of every instance in the project.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud SQL Instance User is the role required when IAM database authentication is used.
option_breakdown.C: Token Creator lets other principals obtain tokens for an account; it is not a permission to log in to a database.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud SQL Viewer reads instance metadata and grants no login to a database.

questions.title: Local code that must run as a service account
questions.summary: A local ADC file created with service account impersonation lets client libraries act as the account without a key.
questions.question: A developer at Bowness Print tests a Python program on a laptop. The program uses Cloud Client Libraries and, to behave as it will in production, must call Google Cloud as the service account print-app. Creating service account keys is blocked by policy. The developer is signed in to gcloud and holds Service Account Token Creator on print-app. What should the developer do?

options.A: Download a key for print-app and point GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS at it
options.B: Set the gcloud property auth/impersonate_service_account to print-app
options.C: Sign in with gcloud auth login, using the email address of print-app
options.D: Create a local ADC file that impersonates print-app

explanation.summary: Client libraries read Application Default Credentials. A local ADC file can be created with impersonation, so the libraries obtain short-lived credentials for the service account with no key.

option_breakdown.A: This needs a service account key, which the policy blocks.
option_breakdown.B: That property changes how gcloud commands authenticate; client libraries read the ADC file and are not affected by it.
option_breakdown.C: A service account has no password and cannot be used for the browser sign-in of gcloud auth login.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. With an impersonating ADC file the client libraries act as print-app using the developer's own sign-in.

questions.title: An engineer who can impersonate every account
questions.summary: Service Account Token Creator granted on a project allows impersonating every service account in it; it belongs on the single account.
questions.question: An access review at Coniston Marine finds that a support engineer can impersonate all twenty-five service accounts in the project cm-fleet, including one that administers production databases. The engineer was only ever meant to impersonate the account log-export. The review shows the engineer holds Service Account Token Creator on the project. What should the administrator do?

options.A: Add an expiry condition to the project-level Token Creator grant
options.B: Grant Token Creator on log-export only, and remove the project-level grant
options.C: Replace the project-level grant with Service Account User on the project
options.D: Disable the twenty-four service accounts the engineer should not use

explanation.summary: A role granted on a project applies to every service account in it. Access to a service account is granted on that account itself, so that it reaches no other account.

option_breakdown.A: Until it expires, the grant would still allow impersonating all twenty-five accounts.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A grant on log-export alone allows impersonating that account and no other.
option_breakdown.C: Service User on the project lets the engineer attach any of the accounts to resources, which is another way to use them all.
option_breakdown.D: Disabling the other accounts would stop the workloads that run as them.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding log-export@cm-fleet.iam.gserviceaccount.com --member="user:support@example.com" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator"
gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding cm-fleet --member="user:support@example.com" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator"

questions.title: What a developer needs before impersonating
questions.summary: Impersonation needs Service Account Token Creator on the account and the Service Account Credentials API enabled.
questions.question: In the new project dv-lab at Dovedale Labs, a developer wants to run gcloud commands as the service account lab-runner by impersonating it. The developer is Viewer on the project and holds no role on any service account. In the project only the Compute Engine and Cloud Storage APIs have been enabled so far. An administrator will make the changes and wants to give the developer as little as possible. Which two things must be put in place? (Choose two.)

options.A: A user-managed key for lab-runner, downloaded by the developer
options.B: The Service Account User role for the developer on lab-runner
options.C: The Owner role for the developer on the project dv-lab
options.D: The Service Account Token Creator role for the developer on lab-runner
options.E: The Service Account Credentials API enabled in the project

explanation.summary: Impersonation means creating short-lived credentials for the account. That takes Token Creator on the account, and the Service Account Credentials API, which issues the credentials, has to be enabled.

option_breakdown.A: A key is a different, long-lived way to authenticate; impersonation exists so that no key is needed.
option_breakdown.B: Service Account User allows attaching the account to resources; it does not allow creating short-lived credentials for it.
option_breakdown.C: Owner is far more than impersonating one account requires, and by itself it does not enable the API.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Token Creator lets the developer create short-lived credentials for lab-runner, which is what impersonation does.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Short-lived credentials are issued by the Service Account Credentials API, so it must be enabled.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud services enable iamcredentials.googleapis.com --project=dv-lab
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding lab-runner@dv-lab.iam.gserviceaccount.com --member="user:dev@example.com" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator"

questions.title: Service Account User, and the impersonation flag fails
questions.summary: Service Account User attaches an account to resources; using the gcloud impersonation flag needs Service Account Token Creator.
questions.question: A release engineer at Malham Brewing holds Service Account User on the service account release-bot and regularly deploys Cloud Run services that run as it. Today the engineer runs a gcloud command with the flag --impersonate-service-account for release-bot and receives a permission error. The engineer needs to run a few commands as release-bot without a key. Which role is missing on release-bot?

options.A: Service Account Token Creator
options.B: Service Account Admin
options.C: Service Account Key Admin
options.D: Workload Identity User

explanation.summary: The two roles cover different acts. Service Account User lets a principal attach the account to a resource. Creating short-lived credentials, which the impersonation flag does, needs Token Creator.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Token Creator lets a principal create short-lived credentials and use the gcloud impersonation flag.
option_breakdown.B: Service Account Admin manages the account itself, such as its description and policy; it does not create credentials for it.
option_breakdown.C: Key Admin creates and deletes keys, which is the long-lived credential the engineer wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.D: Workload Identity User is for GKE workloads acting as the account, not for a person using gcloud.

questions.title: One command as the service account, the rest as yourself
questions.summary: The --impersonate-service-account flag makes a single gcloud command run as a service account without changing the configuration.
questions.question: An engineer at Appletreewick Farms works in gcloud with a personal user account all day. Once, to check what the service account inventory-sync can see, the engineer wants to list Cloud Storage buckets as that account. The engineer holds Service Account Token Creator on it. Every other command, before and after, must keep running as the engineer. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Set the property auth/impersonate_service_account and leave it set
options.B: Create a key for inventory-sync and run gcloud auth activate-service-account
options.C: Create a second gcloud configuration with inventory-sync as its account
options.D: Add the impersonation flag for inventory-sync to that one command

explanation.summary: The flag applies to the command it is given on: gcloud creates short-lived credentials for the service account for that call only. The configuration property applies impersonation to every command.

option_breakdown.A: The property makes every later command run as the service account until it is unset.
option_breakdown.B: A key is a long-lived credential, and activating it switches the active account for the commands that follow.
option_breakdown.C: A service account cannot sign in as a configuration's account without a key, and switching configurations affects later commands.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. With the flag, that one command uses short-lived credentials for the account and nothing else changes.

questions.title: A pipeline account that deploys as another account
questions.summary: One service account impersonates another when it holds Service Account Token Creator on the target account.
questions.question: The CI pipeline of Grassington Software runs on Google Cloud as the service account ci-runner, which has almost no permissions. For production releases the pipeline must obtain short-lived credentials for the service account prod-deployer, which holds the deployment roles. No keys may be created, and ci-runner must not receive the deployment roles itself. What should be granted?

options.A: The deployment roles to ci-runner, on the production project
options.B: Service Account Token Creator to ci-runner, on prod-deployer
options.C: Service Account Token Creator to prod-deployer, on ci-runner
options.D: Service Account Key Admin to ci-runner, on prod-deployer

explanation.summary: A service account can be the caller in an impersonation, like a user. To obtain a token for the target account, the calling account needs Service Account Token Creator on the target.

option_breakdown.A: This gives the pipeline's own account the deployment roles, which the requirement rules out.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. With Token Creator on prod-deployer, ci-runner can obtain short-lived credentials for it.
option_breakdown.C: This is the grant in the wrong direction: it would let prod-deployer impersonate ci-runner.
option_breakdown.D: Key Admin would let the pipeline create keys for prod-deployer, and keys are not allowed.

questions.title: Ending one person's right to impersonate
questions.summary: A principal's access to one service account is revoked by removing its binding from that account's own allow policy.
questions.question: A contractor at Arncliffe Data was granted Service Account Token Creator directly on the service account nightly-etl, and the engagement has ended. Three employees hold the same role on nightly-etl and must keep it. The contractor has no other grants in the project. What should the administrator do to end the contractor's ability to impersonate nightly-etl?

options.A: Disable the service account nightly-etl
options.B: Remove Token Creator from the project's allow policy for the contractor
options.C: Remove the contractor's binding from the allow policy of nightly-etl
options.D: Delete nightly-etl and create it again with the same name

explanation.summary: A service account is a resource with its own allow policy. A grant made on the account is removed there, and removing one member's binding leaves the other members' bindings untouched.

option_breakdown.A: A disabled account cannot be used by anyone, including the three employees and the nightly job.
option_breakdown.B: The grant was made on the service account, so the project's allow policy holds no such binding to remove.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The contractor's access was granted on the account, so it is revoked in that account's allow policy.
option_breakdown.D: A recreated account is a new identity: every binding and every workload using the old one would break.

questions.title: Deciding who may use the project's service accounts
questions.summary: Service Account Admin on a project lets a principal manage access to every service account in it, without rights over other resources.
questions.question: The platform lead at Buckden Robotics must decide who may attach or impersonate each of the forty service accounts in the project br-control, including accounts created later, by granting and revoking roles on those accounts. The lead must not be able to change the project's allow policy or to manage VMs, buckets or other resources. Which grant fits?

options.A: Project IAM Admin on the project br-control
options.B: Service Account Token Creator on the project br-control
options.C: Service Account User on the project br-control
options.D: Service Account Admin on the project br-control

explanation.summary: Managing access to a service account means reading and setting its allow policy, which Service Account Admin provides. Granted on the project, the role applies to all of the project's service accounts.

option_breakdown.A: Project IAM Admin changes the project's allow policy, which is exactly what the lead must not do.
option_breakdown.B: Token Creator on the project lets the lead impersonate every account; it does not let the lead grant access to others.
option_breakdown.C: Service Account User on the project lets the lead attach every account; it does not manage who else may.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Service Account Admin on the project carries the permissions to manage access to its service accounts.

questions.title: A token that works for an hour and then fails
questions.summary: Access tokens from the metadata server expire, so an application asks for a token when it needs one, or lets a client library do so.
questions.question: A custom script on a Compute Engine VM at Langstroth Mills fetches an access token from the metadata server once at start-up, stores it in a variable, and uses it for every call to the Cloud Storage API. About an hour after each start the calls begin to fail with authentication errors, and a restart fixes them for another hour. The VM's service account and its roles are correct. What should the developer change?

options.A: Create a service account key and sign the requests with it
options.B: Request a token from the metadata server whenever one is needed
options.C: Grant the VM's service account the Service Account Token Creator role
options.D: Set the VM's access scope to cloud-platform and restart the VM

explanation.summary: Tokens issued through the metadata server are short-lived. The metadata server caches a token and hands out a fresh one before the old one expires, so a caller that asks each time always has a valid token.

option_breakdown.A: A key would avoid the expiry by adding a long-lived secret to the VM, which is the less secure way round the problem.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Tokens expire after a short time; asking the metadata server again returns a valid one at no real cost.
option_breakdown.C: The account's roles are fine. The calls fail because the stored token has expired, not for lack of a permission.
option_breakdown.D: The calls succeed for the first hour, so scopes are not the obstacle.

questions.title: Two teams' clusters in one project
questions.summary: Clusters in one project share a workload identity pool, so equal namespace and ServiceAccount names are one identity; untrusted clusters belong in separate projects.
questions.question: Two GKE clusters at Hubberholme Data run in the same project. The payments team's cluster has a Pod that uses the Kubernetes ServiceAccount back-ksa in the namespace backend, and that identity is granted access to a sensitive bucket through Workload Identity Federation for GKE. The second cluster belongs to an outside agency, whose administrators can create any namespace and ServiceAccount there. What should be done so that the agency's cluster cannot obtain that access?

options.A: Rename the bucket so that the agency cannot guess its name
options.B: Move the agency's cluster to a separate project
options.C: Give the agency's node pools a different node service account
options.D: Disable the default namespace in the agency's cluster

explanation.summary: Every cluster in a project uses the pool PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog, and IAM does not tell clusters apart: the same namespace and ServiceAccount name in two clusters is the same principal. Separate projects give separate pools.

option_breakdown.A: The agency's workload would hold the same identity as the payments Pod, so it would be authorised whatever the bucket is called.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Clusters in separate projects get different workload identity pools, so the names no longer match one principal.
option_breakdown.C: Workload identity principals come from the namespace and ServiceAccount, not from the node's service account.
option_breakdown.D: The identity in question lives in the namespace backend, which the agency's administrators can create at will.

questions.title: Moving a Standard cluster's workload off the node account
questions.summary: On a Standard cluster, Workload Identity Federation for GKE is enabled on the cluster first and then on the node pool that runs the workload.
questions.question: A workload on an existing GKE Standard cluster at Yockenthwaite Foods reaches Cloud Storage with the node service account. The team wants it to use Workload Identity Federation for GKE instead, with its own Kubernetes ServiceAccount. The feature has never been enabled on the cluster, which has one node pool. Which two steps are needed on the GKE side? (Choose two.)

options.A: Create a key for a service account and store it in a Kubernetes Secret
options.B: Grant the node service account the Editor role on the project
options.C: Convert the cluster's node pool to Spot VMs
options.D: Enable Workload Identity Federation for GKE on the cluster
options.E: Enable it on the node pool, or add a new node pool that has it

explanation.summary: The feature is switched on for the cluster, which creates the project's workload identity pool. Existing node pools are not affected by that, so the pool running the workload must be updated or replaced by a new one.

option_breakdown.A: A key in a Secret is the method that Workload Identity Federation for GKE exists to replace.
option_breakdown.B: More rights for the node account widen access for every Pod on the nodes, the opposite of an identity per workload.
option_breakdown.C: The provisioning model of the nodes has nothing to do with how Pods authenticate.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. It must be enabled at the cluster level before it can be enabled on node pools.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Existing node pools are unaffected by the cluster setting, so the pool is updated or a new one is created.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER_NAME --location=LOCATION --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog
gcloud container node-pools update NODEPOOL_NAME --cluster=CLUSTER_NAME --location=LOCATION --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA

questions.title: Every Pod in one namespace may read the reports bucket
questions.summary: A principal set for a namespace grants a role to all Pods in that namespace, whatever ServiceAccount they use.
questions.question: In a GKE cluster at Cautley Maps, teams keep adding workloads to the namespace reports, each with its own Kubernetes ServiceAccount. Every Pod in that namespace, present and future, must be able to read objects in the bucket cm-reports. Pods in other namespaces must not. Workload Identity Federation for GKE is enabled. To which principal should Storage Object Viewer on the bucket be granted?

options.A: Each Kubernetes ServiceAccount that exists in reports today
options.B: The service account used by the cluster's nodes
options.C: The principal set for the namespace reports
options.D: The principal set for all Pods in the cluster

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Federation for GKE offers principal identifiers for one ServiceAccount, for all Pods in a namespace, and for all Pods in a cluster. The namespace principal set matches the requirement exactly.

option_breakdown.A: Grants to today's ServiceAccounts miss the ones that teams add later.
option_breakdown.B: The node account is shared by Pods of every namespace that run on the nodes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The namespace principal set covers all Pods in reports, regardless of their ServiceAccount.
option_breakdown.D: The cluster-wide principal set would include Pods in every other namespace.

questions.title: Switching a busy node pool without an outage
questions.summary: Updating a node pool enables Workload Identity Federation for GKE for its running workloads at once, cutting them off from the node account; a new node pool allows a gradual move.
questions.question: A GKE Standard cluster at Sedbergh Tools has Workload Identity Federation for GKE enabled on the cluster, but its only node pool still exposes the node service account, which twenty running workloads depend on. The workloads will be migrated to their own identities one at a time over a month, and none may lose access before it has been migrated. How should the engineer proceed?

options.A: Add a node pool with the feature enabled, and move each workload when it is ready
options.B: Update the existing node pool to enable the feature, then migrate the workloads
options.C: Disable the feature on the cluster until all twenty workloads are ready
options.D: Remove the roles from the node service account, then migrate the workloads

explanation.summary: Changing an existing node pool applies to everything running on it immediately: workloads can no longer use the node service account. A separate, enabled node pool lets workloads move over individually.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Workloads stay on the old pool with the node account until each one is ready to move to the new pool.
option_breakdown.B: Modifying the pool immediately stops all twenty workloads from using the node service account, before they are migrated.
option_breakdown.C: The cluster setting does not affect the existing pool, and turning it off would only prevent the migration from starting.
option_breakdown.D: Removing the roles breaks all the workloads that still rely on the node account.

questions.title: A Pod that sometimes gets the node's identity
questions.summary: In a Standard cluster with mixed node pools, a nodeSelector keeps a Pod on node pools that run the GKE metadata server.
questions.question: A GKE Standard cluster at Dentdale Robotics has two node pools: one with Workload Identity Federation for GKE enabled and an older one without it. A Deployment's Pods use a Kubernetes ServiceAccount that has been granted access to a Pub/Sub topic. Pods scheduled on the newer pool publish successfully; replicas that land on the older pool are denied. The older pool must stay as it is for now, and nothing on it may be given new access. What should the engineer change?

options.A: Grant the node service account of the older pool Pub/Sub Publisher
options.B: Increase the number of replicas so that enough Pods succeed
options.C: Add a nodeSelector for nodes that run the GKE metadata server
options.D: Annotate the namespace with the name of the newer node pool

explanation.summary: Only nodes in an enabled node pool run the GKE metadata server. A Pod elsewhere gets the node's identity, so workloads that need their own identity are pinned to enabled nodes with a nodeSelector.

option_breakdown.A: This would make the failing replicas work by giving every Pod on the older nodes publish rights.
option_breakdown.B: More replicas leave the same share of them failing on the older pool.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The selector places the Pods only on node pools that use Workload Identity Federation for GKE.
option_breakdown.D: A namespace annotation does not influence where the scheduler places Pods.

questions.title: One legacy agent that needs the node's own identity
questions.summary: Workload Identity Federation for GKE can be turned off for a single node pool, which then exposes the node service account to its Pods.
questions.question: All workloads in a GKE Standard cluster at Ravenstonedale Energy use Workload Identity Federation for GKE. A newly bought monitoring agent only works when it can obtain the credentials of the node service account from the Compute Engine metadata server. The agent must run in this cluster, and the other workloads must keep their own identities. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Run the agent on a separate node pool where the feature is disabled
options.B: Disable the feature for the whole cluster
options.C: Give the agent's Pods a service account key in a Secret
options.D: Grant the agent's Kubernetes ServiceAccount the Owner role

explanation.summary: The feature is set per node pool. A pool configured to expose the Compute Engine metadata server gives its Pods the node's identity, while Pods on other pools keep their own.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The feature can be selectively disabled on one node pool, which then serves the node's credentials.
option_breakdown.B: Turning it off cluster-wide takes the other workloads' own identities away.
option_breakdown.C: The agent expects the node account from the metadata server; a key file does not provide that.
option_breakdown.D: A role on the Kubernetes ServiceAccount does not change which metadata server the agent's Pod talks to.

questions.title: Every team builds its own workload identity pool
questions.summary: Workload identity pools and providers are managed in one dedicated project so that trusted providers and mappings stay consistent.
questions.question: At Smardale Systems, nine project teams have each created a workload identity pool and provider in their own project for the same external CI system. An audit finds different attribute mappings in every pool and two providers that trust the wrong issuer. The security team wants one consistent, reviewed federation setup for the whole company. How should pools and providers be organised?

options.A: One pool per team project, with a shared naming convention
options.B: All pools and providers in a single dedicated project
options.C: One provider per engineer, in the engineer's sandbox project
options.D: One pool per region, in the project that hosts each region's VMs

explanation.summary: Managing pools and providers in a single dedicated project means only vetted identity providers are trusted and the same attribute mappings and conditions apply for every project that uses them.

option_breakdown.A: Nine separately managed pools are what produced the inconsistent mappings; a naming rule does not review their settings.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A single dedicated project gives one reviewed set of providers, mappings and conditions.
option_breakdown.C: Providers per person multiply the settings to review and tie trust to individual sandboxes.
option_breakdown.D: Federation is not regional; splitting by region again spreads the configuration across projects.

questions.title: No new federation providers outside the central project
questions.summary: The organization policy constraint for workload identity pool providers, set to deny all, prevents providers from being created.
questions.question: Brough Marine now manages all workload identity pools and providers in one dedicated project. Project Owners elsewhere in the organization still have the permission to create a provider in their own projects, and security wants that to be impossible everywhere except in the dedicated project. What should be configured?

options.A: A budget alert on Identity and Access Management usage in every project
options.B: A Cloud Monitoring alert on the creation of workload identity pools
options.C: Removal of the Workload Identity User role from all project Owners
options.D: The provider constraint set to deny all, with an exception for that project

explanation.summary: An organization policy constraint governs which workload identity pool providers may be created. Denying all at the organization blocks creation even for Owners, and an override on the dedicated project keeps it working there.

option_breakdown.A: Federation is not billed in a way a budget would catch, and a budget cannot block the creation of anything.
option_breakdown.B: An alert reports a provider after it has been created; the aim is that it cannot be created.
option_breakdown.C: Workload Identity User lets a principal act as a service account; it is not the permission to create providers.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The constraint with a deny-all rule prevents the creation of new providers wherever it applies.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud resource-manager org-policies deny iam.workloadIdentityPoolProviders --organization=ORG_ID all

questions.title: A dashboard that lists topics but must not read messages
questions.summary: Pub/Sub Viewer lets a principal see topics and subscriptions without publishing or consuming messages.
questions.question: An inventory tool at Thwaite Logistics runs as a service account and must list the Pub/Sub topics and subscriptions of the project tl-events and show their settings. It must not be able to publish messages, pull messages from any subscription, or change any topic or subscription. Which predefined role should the service account be granted on the project?

options.A: Pub/Sub Subscriber
options.B: Pub/Sub Viewer
options.C: Pub/Sub Editor
options.D: Pub/Sub Publisher

explanation.summary: Pub/Sub has separate predefined roles for viewing, publishing, subscribing and editing. The viewer role gives read access to the resources' configuration only.

option_breakdown.A: Subscriber lets the tool consume messages from subscriptions, which it must not do.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Pub/Sub Viewer provides access to view topics and subscriptions and nothing else.
option_breakdown.C: Editor lets the tool create, change and delete topics and subscriptions.
option_breakdown.D: Publisher lets the tool publish messages to topics, which it must not do.

questions.title: A build pipeline that pushes images
questions.summary: Artifact Registry Writer lets a principal read and write artifacts without administering repositories.
questions.question: The build pipeline of Muker Software runs as a service account and must push container images to the Artifact Registry repository apps, and pull base images from it. It must not be able to delete images, delete the repository or change the repository's IAM policy. Which predefined role should the service account be granted on the repository?

options.A: Artifact Registry Reader
options.B: Artifact Registry Writer
options.C: Artifact Registry Administrator
options.D: Storage Admin

explanation.summary: Artifact Registry's predefined roles step up from reading, to reading and writing, to administering. Pushing an image is a write, so the writer role is the narrowest that fits.

option_breakdown.A: Reader can pull images but cannot push new ones.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Artifact Registry Writer can read and write artifacts, which covers pulling and pushing.
option_breakdown.C: Administrator can also delete artifacts and repositories and change access, which the pipeline must not do.
option_breakdown.D: Storage Admin is a Cloud Storage role and gives no access to an Artifact Registry repository.

questions.title: A project Editor who cannot read a secret
questions.summary: The basic Editor role does not include reading secret values; that needs Secret Manager Secret Accessor.
questions.question: A developer at Keld Analytics holds the basic Editor role on the project ka-dev and assumes it covers everything short of IAM changes. When the developer tries to read the value of the secret db-password in Secret Manager, the request is denied. The developer needs to read this one secret and no other. What should be granted?

options.A: Secret Manager Secret Accessor on the secret db-password
options.B: Secret Manager Viewer on the project ka-dev
options.C: Secret Manager Admin on the project ka-dev
options.D: The basic Owner role on the project ka-dev

explanation.summary: Access to a secret's value is a separate permission that the Editor and Viewer basic roles do not contain. Secret Accessor carries it, and it can be granted on a single secret.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Secret Accessor on that one secret lets the developer read its value and no other secret's.
option_breakdown.B: Secret Manager Viewer shows the metadata of secrets; it does not allow reading a value.
option_breakdown.C: Secret Manager Admin on the project lets the developer read and manage every secret in it.
option_breakdown.D: Owner does include the permission, along with full control of the whole project.

questions.title: An application that encrypts with one key
questions.summary: Using a key to encrypt and decrypt is the key user's role, Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter, not a key management role.
questions.question: A payment service at Gunnerside Pay runs as a service account and calls Cloud KMS to encrypt and decrypt card tokens with the key tokens-key. The service must not be able to rotate, disable or destroy the key, or to create other keys. Which role should the service account be granted on tokens-key?

options.A: Cloud KMS Admin
options.B: Cloud KMS Viewer
options.C: Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter
options.D: Owner

explanation.summary: Cloud KMS separates key managers, who control a key's lifecycle, from key users, who perform cryptographic operations with it. An application that encrypts and decrypts is a key user.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud KMS Admin manages key lifecycles: rotation, state changes and destruction, which the service must not do.
option_breakdown.B: Viewer can see keys and their metadata but cannot use a key to encrypt or decrypt.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Encrypter/Decrypter authorizes using the key for encryption and decryption, and no key management.
option_breakdown.D: Owner includes key management and everything else in the project.

questions.title: A key custodian who must never decrypt
questions.summary: Separation of duties in Cloud KMS gives key managers the Cloud KMS Admin role and keeps the encrypt and decrypt role away from them.
questions.question: The security officer at Arkengarth Bank creates key rings and keys, sets rotation schedules, and disables or destroys key versions. Under the bank's separation of duties rule, the role the officer holds must not itself contain any permission to decrypt data. Applications hold their own roles for using the keys. Which role should the officer be granted on the key project?

options.A: Cloud KMS Admin
options.B: Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter
options.C: Owner
options.D: Cloud KMS CryptoKey Decrypter

explanation.summary: Key managers are authorised to manage key lifecycles, for example with Cloud KMS Admin. Key users perform cryptographic operations with a separate role, so one person never holds both.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Cloud KMS Admin manages key lifecycles: creation, deletion, rotation and state changes.
option_breakdown.B: This is the key user's role; it allows decrypting data and does not manage keys.
option_breakdown.C: Owner covers key management but also lets the officer use the keys, which breaks the rule.
option_breakdown.D: This role allows exactly what the officer must never do, and no key management.

questions.title: A team lead who may only create service accounts
questions.summary: The Create Service Accounts role lets a principal create service accounts; granting them access to the project needs a further role.
questions.question: A team lead at Whaw Robotics must create service accounts for new workloads in the project wr-line. Granting those accounts roles on the project stays with the security team, and the lead must not be able to change the project's allow policy, create keys or manage other resources. Which role should the lead be granted on the project?

options.A: Create Service Accounts
options.B: Project IAM Admin
options.C: Service Account Key Admin
options.D: Editor

explanation.summary: Creating service accounts has its own predefined role. Giving the new accounts access to the project is a separate act that needs Project IAM Admin, so the two duties can be held by different people.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The Create Service Accounts role provides the permissions to create service accounts and no more.
option_breakdown.B: Project IAM Admin changes the project's allow policy, which is the security team's job, and does not create accounts.
option_breakdown.C: Key Admin creates and deletes service account keys, which the lead must not do.
option_breakdown.D: Editor can create service accounts, along with keys and nearly every other resource in the project.

questions.title: The script creates accounts but cannot grant them roles
questions.summary: Creating a service account and granting it access to the project are separate permissions; the second needs Project IAM Admin.
questions.question: A provisioning script at Oughtershaw Tech runs as a service account that holds the Create Service Accounts role on the project ot-apps. For each new workload it creates a service account, which works, and then tries to grant that account a role on ot-apps, which fails with a permission error. Which of these roles must the script's service account also hold on ot-apps for the second step, without gaining rights over the project's other resources?

options.A: Service Account User
options.B: Service Account Key Admin
options.C: Project IAM Admin
options.D: Editor

explanation.summary: The Create Service Accounts role covers creating the account. Adding a role binding for it on the project is a change to the project's allow policy, which takes Project IAM Admin.

option_breakdown.A: Service Account User allows attaching accounts to resources; it does not change the project's allow policy.
option_breakdown.B: Key Admin manages keys for service accounts and grants nothing on the project.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Granting newly created service accounts access to the project also needs the Project IAM Admin role.
option_breakdown.D: Editor cannot change the project's allow policy, and it brings change rights on most other resources.

questions.title: A vendor's engineer who asks for a service account login
questions.summary: A service account has no password and cannot sign in to the console; a person needs a user identity.
questions.question: A monitoring vendor's engineer needs to sign in to the Google Cloud console of Askrigg Dairy for two weeks to review dashboards. The engineer asks Askrigg to create a service account and send its email address and a password, as the vendor does on other platforms. What should the administrator do?

options.A: Create the service account and set a password for it in the IAM page
options.B: Create the service account and send the engineer a key file to sign in with
options.C: Give the engineer a user identity and grant that identity the viewing role
options.D: Create the service account and add it to the engineer's Google group

explanation.summary: Service accounts represent workloads, not people. They have no password and cannot be used for browser-based sign-in, so a person who must use the console needs a user account or a federated user identity.

option_breakdown.A: A service account has no password, so there is nothing to set.
option_breakdown.B: A key authenticates programs to APIs; it cannot be used to sign in to the console, and it is a long-lived secret to hand out.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A person signs in as a user, and the user identity is granted the role for the two weeks.
option_breakdown.D: Group membership does not give a service account a way to sign in through a browser.

questions.title: Pods lose access after the feature is enabled
questions.summary: Enabling Workload Identity Federation for GKE grants nothing; each workload's Kubernetes identity must be given its own IAM access.
questions.question: Until last week the Pods of the service exporter in a GKE Standard cluster at Marske Media wrote to a Cloud Storage bucket through the node service account. The team then enabled Workload Identity Federation for GKE on the cluster and its node pool, and the Pods have been denied ever since. The Pods run as the Kubernetes ServiceAccount exporter-ksa in the namespace data. The Pods need to write objects to that bucket. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Disable the feature again, because it cannot be combined with Cloud Storage
options.B: Grant the node service account Storage Admin on the project
options.C: Restart the Pods so that they pick up the node service account again
options.D: Grant the principal for exporter-ksa Storage Object User on the bucket

explanation.summary: With the feature on, Pods no longer use the node service account: they authenticate as their Kubernetes ServiceAccount. Enabling the feature creates that identity but gives it no permissions.

option_breakdown.A: The feature works with Cloud Storage; the Pods are denied because their new identity has not been granted anything.
option_breakdown.B: The Pods no longer act as the node account, so its roles do not reach them, and a project-wide admin role is far too broad.
option_breakdown.C: After a restart the Pods still authenticate as their Kubernetes ServiceAccount, not as the node.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The Kubernetes ServiceAccount's principal needs an allow policy binding on the bucket.

questions.title: A Windows service that only has Kerberos tickets
questions.summary: An ambient credential that federation does not accept can first be exchanged at an identity provider for a token that it does accept.
questions.question: A Windows service in the data centre of Ingleton Works must call Google Cloud APIs. It runs in an Active Directory domain and can obtain Kerberos tickets, which Workload Identity Federation does not accept. The company also runs Active Directory Federation Services, which supports Integrated Windows Authentication. Security wants no service account key on the server. What should the engineer set up?

options.A: A service account key stored in the Windows credential store
options.B: A token from AD FS obtained with Kerberos, exchanged through Workload Identity Federation
options.C: A workforce identity pool, with the service signing in as a user
options.D: A Cloud VPN tunnel, so that the service counts as running inside Google Cloud

explanation.summary: When the ambient credential is of an unsupported type, an additional token exchange can convert it: here Kerberos to a JWT access token from AD FS, which Workload Identity Federation then exchanges for short-lived Google credentials.

option_breakdown.A: This is the service account key that security wants to avoid, wherever it is stored.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Kerberos is exchanged at AD FS for a token that Workload Identity Federation accepts, with no key.
option_breakdown.C: Workforce pools are for people signing in to the console and tools, not for a service's identity.
option_breakdown.D: A network tunnel does not give a workload a Google identity; it still has to authenticate.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc adfs --workload-identity-pool=onprem --location=global --issuer-uri=https://adfs.example.com/adfs --attribute-mapping=google.subject=assertion.sub

questions.title: One secret to rotate, or two
questions.summary: An application that already authenticates to an OIDC or SAML provider can exchange that provider's tokens through federation and needs no service account key.
questions.question: An on-premises application at Clapham Print already authenticates to the company's OpenID Connect identity provider with a client secret, which is rotated every quarter. The application must now also call Google Cloud APIs. The security team wants to keep the number of secrets that need rotation as low as possible. How should the application get Google credentials?

options.A: Exchange the identity provider's tokens through Workload Identity Federation
options.B: Use a service account key stored next to the client secret
options.C: Use an API key restricted to the application's IP address
options.D: Use the personal credentials of the application's owner

explanation.summary: The application can reuse the tokens its identity provider already issues. Federation exchanges them for short-lived Google credentials, so the client secret stays the only secret to rotate.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Using the existing provider's tokens with federation adds no second secret.
option_breakdown.B: A key next to the client secret means two secrets to store, protect and rotate.
option_breakdown.C: An API key is another long-lived secret, and most Google Cloud APIs need an identity, not an API key.
option_breakdown.D: A person's credentials tie the application to one employee and cannot be rotated like a workload secret.

questions.title: Two providers in one pool, one name in the logs
questions.summary: Each workload identity pool should have a single provider, so that subjects from different providers cannot collide.
questions.question: A workload identity pool at Horton Freight has two providers: the company's own identity provider and a partner's. Both map their subject claim to google.subject, and both issue the subject build-agent. In Cloud Audit Logs the company cannot tell whether a call was made by its own build agent or the partner's. Both parties must keep access. How should the federation be restructured?

options.A: Keep one pool and give both providers the same attribute condition
options.B: Create a separate pool for each provider, with one provider in each
options.C: Keep one pool and delete the partner's provider
options.D: Create a service account key for the partner's build agent

explanation.summary: Within a pool, equal google.subject values from different providers are the same IAM principal. A pool per provider keeps the identities distinct, and so distinguishable in audit logs.

option_breakdown.A: The same condition on both providers does nothing to keep their subjects apart.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. With one provider per pool, the two build agents become different principals.
option_breakdown.C: The partner must keep access, and deleting its provider removes it.
option_breakdown.D: A key gives the partner a long-lived secret, the thing federation is used to avoid.

questions.title: A new hire inherits a former contractor's access
questions.summary: Attribute mappings should use an attribute that is never reused, such as a unique ID, not an email address.
questions.question: A workload identity provider at Settle Robotics maps the external identity's email address to google.subject. The external identity provider reuses email addresses: a deleted contractor's address was later given to a new account, and that new identity turned out to have the old one's access to a service account in Google Cloud. What should the engineer change to prevent this in future?

options.A: Map google.subject to a unique ID that the identity provider never reuses
options.B: Map google.subject to the identity's display name, not its email address
options.C: Shorten the lifetime of the tokens that the identity provider issues
options.D: Create a new pool every time an external identity is deleted

explanation.summary: Federation has no directory of its own: two tokens whose claims map to the same subject are the same principal. If the mapped attribute can be reused, a later identity inherits earlier bindings.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. An attribute that cannot be reused over time, like a unique user ID, keeps old bindings from matching new identities.
option_breakdown.B: Display names are reused and changed even more freely than email addresses.
option_breakdown.C: Token lifetime does not change which principal a token is mapped to.
option_breakdown.D: A pool per deletion is unmanageable, and the mapping itself would still be ambiguous.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers update-oidc PROVIDER_ID --workload-identity-pool=POOL_ID --location=global --attribute-mapping=google.subject=assertion.sub

questions.title: A GKE Pod reading one bucket without keys
questions.summary: Workload Identity Federation for GKE: grant the role to the Kubernetes ServiceAccount's principal on the resource, and run the Pod as that ServiceAccount.
questions.question: Teams at Mirelle Foods deploy a report generator to a GKE Standard cluster with Workload Identity Federation for GKE enabled on the cluster and its node pools. The Pods must read objects in one Cloud Storage bucket, no service account keys may exist, and no other workload on the nodes may gain that access. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Make the bucket readable by allAuthenticatedUsers and restrict it with a firewall rule.
options.B: Grant Storage Object Viewer on the bucket to the principal identifier of the app's Kubernetes ServiceAccount.
options.C: Set serviceAccountName in the Deployment's Pod spec to that Kubernetes ServiceAccount.
options.D: Grant Storage Object Viewer on the bucket to the node pool's service account.
options.E: Create a key for a Google service account and mount it into the Pods as a Kubernetes Secret.

explanation.summary: With Workload Identity Federation for GKE, IAM can name a Kubernetes ServiceAccount directly as a principal. Granting the role on the bucket to that principal, and running the Pods as that ServiceAccount, gives only those Pods the access, with no keys.

option_breakdown.A: allAuthenticatedUsers is any Google account on the internet, and VPC firewall rules don't govern access to the Cloud Storage API.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The principal://…/ns/NAMESPACE/sa/KSA identifier lets IAM grant the role to exactly this workload, on exactly this bucket.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The Pods only get the workload identity if they run as the Kubernetes ServiceAccount named in the grant.
option_breakdown.D: Every Pod on those nodes that falls back to the node identity would share the grant, which the stem rules out.
option_breakdown.E: A key is a long-lived secret, and the stem forbids service account keys.

questions.title: Terraform from GitHub Actions without a key
questions.summary: A workload identity pool with a GitHub OIDC provider, limited by an attribute condition, lets the repository's workflow impersonate the deploy service account with short-lived tokens.
questions.question: Corwen Analytics applies Terraform from GitHub Actions in the repository corwen/infra. Today the workflow uses a service account key stored as a GitHub secret, and security wants the key deleted while the pipeline keeps applying as the deploy service account. Only that repository may use it. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Keep the key but rotate it every 24 hours with a scheduled Cloud Run job that updates the GitHub secret.
options.B: Grant the pool's principal set for the repository Workload Identity User on the deploy service account.
options.C: Grant the members of the GitHub organization the Owner role on the project that Terraform manages.
options.D: Create a workload identity pool with an OIDC provider for GitHub, and an attribute condition that matches the corwen/infra repository.
options.E: Move the key into Secret Manager and have the workflow read it from there at the start of each run.

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Federation trusts the OIDC token GitHub issues to each run. The provider's attribute condition limits which repositories are accepted, and Workload Identity User on the service account lets that principal set impersonate it, so no key is needed.

option_breakdown.A: Rotation shortens a key's life but keeps keys, which security wants gone.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. This binding lets the federated identities of that repository impersonate the deploy service account.
option_breakdown.C: Owner to people is far beyond least privilege and doesn't let a workflow authenticate at all.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The pool and provider accept GitHub's OIDC tokens, and the condition rejects every repository except corwen/infra.
option_breakdown.E: The key still exists and still works if leaked; moving it doesn't meet the requirement to delete it.

questions.title: VM admin rights in every development project
questions.summary: A role granted on a folder is inherited by every project in it, including projects created there later, and by nothing outside it.
questions.question: Atherton Bank keeps its 30 development projects in a Development folder and its production projects in a separate Production folder. The platform group must start, stop and resize VMs in every development project, including projects created next month, and in no production project. What should you do?

options.A: Grant Compute Instance Admin (v1) to the group on each of the 30 development projects.
options.B: Grant Compute Instance Admin (v1) to the group on the organization.
options.C: Grant Compute Instance Admin (v1) to the group on the Development folder.
options.D: Grant the Editor basic role to the group on the Development folder.

explanation.summary: IAM policies inherit down the resource hierarchy. A binding on the Development folder applies to every project under it now and later, and not to the Production folder.

option_breakdown.A: Per-project grants work today but miss next month's projects until someone remembers to add them.
option_breakdown.B: An organization grant is inherited by the Production folder too, which the group must not reach.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The folder binding covers all current and future development projects and stops at the folder's edge.
option_breakdown.D: Editor allows changes to almost every service, far more than managing VMs.

questions.title: Creating VMs that run as an app service account
questions.summary: Creating a VM that runs as a service account needs a role to create instances and Service Account User on that service account.
questions.question: Developers at Kirkwall Labs must create Compute Engine VMs in project lab-apps that run as the service account app-runner@lab-apps.iam.gserviceaccount.com. They must not be able to manage service accounts or keys, or run VMs as any other service account. Which two roles should you grant them? (Choose two.)

options.A: Service Account Token Creator on the app-runner service account
options.B: Compute Instance Admin (v1) on the lab-apps project
options.C: Service Account Admin on the app-runner service account
options.D: Service Account User on the lab-apps project
options.E: Service Account User on the app-runner service account

explanation.summary: Attaching a service account to a VM needs iam.serviceAccounts.actAs on that service account, which Service Account User grants. Creating the VM needs a Compute Engine role such as Compute Instance Admin (v1).

option_breakdown.A: Token Creator lets them mint tokens as the service account, which isn't what attaching it to a VM needs and is wider than required.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. It lets the developers create and manage the VMs themselves.
option_breakdown.C: Service Account Admin lets them manage the service account itself, which the stem forbids.
option_breakdown.D: On the project, it allows acting as every service account in the project, not just app-runner.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Granted on app-runner only, it allows actAs on that one service account.

questions.title: Trimming a service account that has too much access
questions.summary: IAM role recommendations compare granted permissions with the ones used over the last 90 days and suggest a smaller role.
questions.question: An audit at Stanway Logistics found that the service account behind a nightly export job has the Editor role on its project, granted two years ago. The team doesn't know which permissions the job actually uses and wants evidence-based least privilege without breaking the job. What should you use?

options.A: IAM role recommendations for the service account, then apply the suggested role.
options.B: An IAM deny policy that blocks every permission except storage.objects.create.
options.C: Remove Editor and add roles back one at a time as the job fails each night.
options.D: The Policy Troubleshooter to check whether the service account can call one API.

explanation.summary: The IAM recommender, part of Active Assist, looks at the permissions a principal used over the last 90 days and recommends replacing an over-broad role with a smaller one that still covers that use.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The recommendation is based on observed use, so the smaller role still covers what the job does.
option_breakdown.B: Guessing a single permission for a deny policy, without data, is likely to break the job.
option_breakdown.C: Trial and error breaks the job repeatedly, which the team wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.D: The Troubleshooter explains one access decision; it doesn't say which permissions are unused.

questions.title: Only the break-glass group may delete projects
questions.summary: An IAM deny policy at the organization can deny a permission to everyone, with exception principals, and it overrides any allow policy below it.
questions.question: After a project was deleted by mistake, Holloway Trust wants nobody in the organization to be able to delete a project, even with Owner, except members of the break-glass group. Existing allow policies across hundreds of projects must stay as they are. What should you do?

options.A: Add a lien to one project so that people can see that deletion is discouraged.
options.B: Create a custom Owner role without the delete permission in each project and use it.
options.C: Remove the Owner role from every principal in every project in the organization.
options.D: Attach a deny policy for project deletion at the organization, exempting break-glass.

explanation.summary: Deny policies are evaluated before allow policies and are inherited down the hierarchy. One at the organization denies project deletion everywhere, with exception principals for the break-glass group.

option_breakdown.A: A lien protects only the project it's placed on, and anyone with the right permission can remove it.
option_breakdown.B: Replacing Owner project by project rewrites the allow policies the stem says must stay.
option_breakdown.C: Removing Owner everywhere changes hundreds of allow policies and breaks legitimate admin work.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The deny applies to every project under the organization, whatever roles people hold, with the group exempted.

questions.title: Running gcloud as the deploy service account
questions.summary: Service account impersonation needs Service Account Token Creator on that account; gcloud then uses short-lived tokens with --impersonate-service-account.
questions.question: A release manager at Brockley Systems must sometimes run gcloud commands as deploy-sa to test what the pipeline can do. No key for deploy-sa may exist, and the release manager's own account should not get the deploy roles. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Grant the release manager the same roles that deploy-sa has.
options.B: Create a key for deploy-sa and activate it with gcloud auth activate-service-account.
options.C: Run the commands with --impersonate-service-account=deploy-sa, or set auth/impersonate_service_account.
options.D: Grant the release manager Service Account Token Creator on deploy-sa.
options.E: Grant the release manager Service Account Admin on the project.

explanation.summary: Token Creator on a service account lets a user obtain short-lived tokens for it. gcloud's impersonation flag or property makes each command call APIs as the service account, with no key.

option_breakdown.A: Copying the roles to the user is what the stem rules out, and it doesn't test the service account's own access.
option_breakdown.B: A key is exactly what must not exist.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. gcloud then acts as deploy-sa with short-lived credentials.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Token Creator on deploy-sa is the permission impersonation needs.
option_breakdown.E: Service Account Admin manages service accounts; it doesn't by itself allow acting as one, and it's too broad.

questions.title: An app on AWS reading Cloud Storage without keys
questions.summary: A workload identity pool with an AWS provider exchanges the EC2 instance's AWS credentials for short-lived Google tokens, so no service account key is needed.
