questions.question: A reporting app at Nantwich Freight runs on Amazon EC2 instances with an IAM role in AWS account 111122223333. It must read objects from a Cloud Storage bucket in Google Cloud. Security forbids service account keys outside Google Cloud. What should you set up?

options.A: A service account key, kept in AWS Secrets Manager and read by the app at start-up
options.B: A Cloud VPN tunnel between the AWS VPC and the Google Cloud VPC that the app routes through
options.C: A workload identity pool with an AWS provider, and IAM access for the EC2 role's principal
options.D: A signed URL for each object in the bucket, regenerated by hand every week for the app

explanation.summary: Workload Identity Federation trusts AWS as an identity provider. The app exchanges its AWS credentials for a short-lived Google access token, and IAM grants access to the federated principal or to a service account it impersonates.

option_breakdown.A: A stored key is still a key outside Google Cloud, which is forbidden.
option_breakdown.B: A VPN connects networks; the app would still need credentials to call the Cloud Storage API.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The EC2 role authenticates through the pool, and no long-lived Google credential exists.
option_breakdown.D: Hand-made signed URLs don't scale and depend on someone generating them each week.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-aws aws-prod --workload-identity-pool=aws-pool \
  --location=global --account-id=111122223333

questions.title: GKE Pods reaching a private Cloud SQL instance without keys
questions.summary: Run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy beside the app and give the Kubernetes ServiceAccount's principal Cloud SQL Client through Workload Identity Federation for GKE: IAM-authorized connections, no keys.
questions.question: Your application runs on a GKE Autopilot cluster and must connect to a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance that has only a private IP address. Service account keys are not allowed, and connections must be authorized through IAM rather than by IP address range. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Grant Cloud SQL Client to the principal of the app's Kubernetes ServiceAccount.
options.B: Grant the Cloud SQL Admin role to the default Compute Engine service account of the nodes.
options.C: Run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar container in the application's Pods.
options.D: Create a service account key, store it in a Kubernetes Secret, and mount the Secret into every Pod.
options.E: Add the cluster's Pod IP address range to the authorized networks of the Cloud SQL instance.

explanation.summary: The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy authorizes each connection with IAM and encrypts it. With Workload Identity Federation for GKE, the Kubernetes ServiceAccount's principal gets Cloud SQL Client directly, so the proxy needs no key.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets the Pods act as that principal, which needs only Cloud SQL Client.
option_breakdown.B: Admin is far more than connecting needs, and Autopilot workloads shouldn't rely on the node's service account.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The proxy connects with IAM authorization over an encrypted tunnel to the instance's private IP.
option_breakdown.D: Keys are forbidden by the stem, and a mounted key is a long-lived secret that can leak.
option_breakdown.E: Authorized networks allow by IP range, which the stem rules out, and they apply to public IP connections.

questions.title: Analysts querying another project's dataset
questions.summary: To query data in another project and bill the query to their own, users need BigQuery Data Viewer on the dataset and BigQuery Job User on the project that runs the job.
questions.question: Analysts in the group analysts@example.com run queries from the project analytics-prj, which must pay for the queries. The data is in the dataset sales in the project data-prj. The analysts may read only that dataset. You want to follow the principle of least privilege. Which two roles should you grant? (Choose two.)

options.A: BigQuery Job User on the data-prj project
options.B: BigQuery Job User on the analytics-prj project
options.C: BigQuery Admin on the analytics-prj project
options.D: BigQuery Data Viewer on the whole data-prj project
options.E: BigQuery Data Viewer on the sales dataset

explanation.summary: Reading data and running jobs are separate permissions. Data Viewer on the dataset lets the analysts read only sales; Job User on analytics-prj lets them run query jobs there, so that project pays.

option_breakdown.A: Jobs would run and be billed in data-prj, which isn't the project that must pay.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Query jobs run, and are billed, in the project where the analysts hold Job User.
option_breakdown.C: Admin can manage every dataset and job in the project, far more than querying needs.
option_breakdown.D: A project-level grant reads every dataset in data-prj, not just sales.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. A dataset-level grant reads that dataset and no other.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding analytics-prj \
  --member=group:analysts@example.com --role=roles/bigquery.jobUser
bq add-iam-policy-binding --member=group:analysts@example.com \
  --role=roles/bigquery.dataViewer data-prj:sales

questions.title: An internal web app for one group, without a VPN
questions.summary: Identity-Aware Proxy on the load balancer's backend service checks each user's identity; grant the group the IAP-secured Web App User role.
questions.question: An internal reporting web app runs on a managed instance group behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Only employees in the group finance@example.com may use it, from anywhere and without a VPN, signing in with their Google accounts. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.A: Enable IAP on the backend service, and grant the group the IAP-secured Web App User role.
options.B: Add a Cloud Armor security policy that allows only the employees' home IP addresses.
options.C: Grant the finance group the Compute Viewer role on the project of the load balancer.
options.D: Move the app behind an internal Application Load Balancer, and give the group a VPN.

explanation.summary: IAP checks each request's identity at the load balancer and lets through only principals who hold IAP-secured Web App User on the resource. Users sign in with their Google accounts from anywhere.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. IAP enforces sign-in and the group's role at the load balancer, with no VPN.
option_breakdown.B: Home IP addresses change and aren't identities, so an allow-list is fragile and coarse.
option_breakdown.C: Compute Viewer lets people see resources in the console; it doesn't control access to the app.
option_breakdown.D: The stem rules out a VPN, and an internal load balancer isn't reachable from anywhere.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud iap web enable --resource-type=backend-services --service=reports-bs
gcloud iap web add-iam-policy-binding --resource-type=backend-services --service=reports-bs \
  --member=group:finance@example.com --role=roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor

questions.title: Cloud Build deploying to Cloud Run in another project
questions.summary: A deployer needs a Cloud Run role in the target project and Service Account User (actAs) on the runtime service account it deploys the service to run as.
questions.question: A Cloud Build pipeline in the project ci-prj builds images and must deploy them to the Cloud Run service checkout in the project app-prj. The service runs as runtime@app-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com, and the build runs as builder@ci-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com. app-prj can already pull the images. Following the principle of least privilege, which two grants should you make? (Choose two.)

options.A: Service Account User on the runtime service account, to the builder service account
options.B: Cloud Run Developer on app-prj, to the builder service account
options.C: Cloud Run Admin on ci-prj, to the runtime service account
options.D: Service Account Token Creator on the builder service account, to the runtime service account
options.E: Owner on app-prj, to the builder service account

explanation.summary: Deploying a revision needs permission to update the service, and permission to act as the service account the revision will run as. Cloud Run Developer gives the first; Service Account User on the runtime account gives the second.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Deploying a service that runs as runtime@ requires actAs on that account.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud Run Developer can deploy revisions but can't change the service's IAM policy.
option_breakdown.C: The runtime account doesn't deploy anything, and ci-prj has no Cloud Run service to manage.
option_breakdown.D: That lets the runtime account mint tokens for the builder, the wrong direction and not needed.
option_breakdown.E: Owner would work, but it grants control of the whole project.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding app-prj --role=roles/run.developer \
  --member=serviceAccount:builder@ci-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding runtime@app-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role=roles/iam.serviceAccountUser --member=serviceAccount:builder@ci-prj.iam.gserviceaccount.com

questions.title: A VM whose service account has the role but still gets a 403
questions.summary: Access scopes limit what a VM's service account tokens can do. Google recommends the cloud-platform scope with IAM roles; changing scopes needs the VM to be stopped.
questions.question: An application on a Compute Engine VM writes rows to BigQuery and fails with a 403 insufficient authentication scopes error. The VM runs as a user-managed service account that holds BigQuery Data Editor on the dataset, and it was created with the default access scopes. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the VM's service account the BigQuery Admin role on the whole project.
options.B: Change the access scopes while the VM runs; new tokens get them within minutes.
options.C: Create a key for the service account, and point GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS at it.
options.D: Stop the VM, set its access scope to cloud-platform, and then start it again.

explanation.summary: The default access scopes don't include BigQuery, so the VM's tokens can't call it whatever the IAM roles say. Google recommends the cloud-platform scope and controlling access with IAM roles. A VM's scopes can only be changed while it is stopped.

option_breakdown.A: The error is about scopes, not roles, so a broader role changes nothing.
option_breakdown.B: A VM's service account and scopes can't be changed while it is running.
option_breakdown.C: A key works around the scope with a long-lived secret, which Google advises against.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. With the cloud-platform scope, the service account's IAM roles decide access.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances stop loader-1 --zone=us-central1-a
gcloud compute instances set-service-account loader-1 --zone=us-central1-a \
  --service-account=loader@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com --scopes=cloud-platform
gcloud compute instances start loader-1 --zone=us-central1-a

questions.title: Firewall administrators for every network host project
questions.summary: A role granted on a folder is inherited by present and future projects in it; firewall rules need Compute Security Admin, not Network Admin.
questions.question: Marchmont Energy keeps its Shared VPC host projects in the folder Networking, and adds a new host project there for each region it enters. The firewall team must create and change firewall rules in every host project, including future ones, with no per-project grants. The team must have no rights in projects outside that folder. What should be granted to the team's group?

options.A: Compute Network Admin on the folder Networking
options.B: Compute Security Admin on each existing host project
options.C: Compute Security Admin on the folder Networking
options.D: Compute Security Admin on the organization

explanation.summary: Allow policies are inherited down the hierarchy, so a grant on the folder reaches every project in it, now and later. Firewall rules are managed with Compute Security Admin; Network Admin excludes them.

option_breakdown.A: Network Admin controls networks, subnets and routes but not firewall rules, which is the one thing the team needs.
option_breakdown.B: Per-project grants miss every host project added later and are the per-project work the company wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Security Admin manages firewall rules, and the folder grant is inherited by all its projects, present and future.
option_breakdown.D: A grant on the organization is inherited by every project in the company, far outside the Networking folder.

questions.title: A bucket readable by one group, through IAM alone
questions.summary: Uniform bucket-level access turns off ACLs so that only IAM grants access; a bucket-level role then gives one group read access.
questions.question: Objects in the bucket hm-contracts at Hartsmere Legal have object ACLs added over the years, and nobody knows any more who can read what. From today, access to the bucket must be decided by IAM alone, and only the group legal-readers may read its objects. Other buckets in the project must not be affected. Which two actions should the engineer take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Enable uniform bucket-level access on hm-contracts
options.B: Grant legal-readers Storage Object Viewer on the whole project
options.C: Add an object ACL entry for legal-readers to every object
options.D: Make the objects public and share them through signed URLs
options.E: Grant legal-readers Storage Object Viewer on hm-contracts

explanation.summary: IAM and ACLs work in parallel, and either one can grant access. Uniform bucket-level access disables ACLs in the bucket, so the IAM policy is the whole story, and a role on the bucket reaches that bucket only.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. It disables ACLs for everything in the bucket, so access is then granted exclusively through IAM.
option_breakdown.B: A project-level grant would let the group read objects in every bucket of the project.
option_breakdown.C: More ACL entries keep the ACL system in use, when access is supposed to be decided by IAM alone.
option_breakdown.D: Public objects can be read by anyone, the opposite of restricting them to one group.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. The role on this bucket lets the group read its objects and nothing in other buckets.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud storage buckets update gs://hm-contracts --uniform-bucket-level-access
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://hm-contracts --member="group:legal-readers@example.com" --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"

questions.title: A managed instance group that stopped creating VMs
questions.summary: The Google APIs Service Agent runs internal Compute Engine processes such as managed instance groups, and needs its role on the project.
questions.question: After an IAM clean-up in the project kd-web at Kildare Media, a managed instance group can no longer create VMs when it scales out or replaces an unhealthy instance. The audit log shows that the clean-up removed the Instance Group Manager Service Agent role from the account PROJECT_NUMBER@cloudservices.gserviceaccount.com. The instance template, quotas and VMs' own service account are unchanged. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Attach a new user-managed service account to the instance template
options.B: Grant that account the role that the clean-up removed from it
options.C: Recreate the managed instance group from the same instance template
options.D: Grant the VMs' service account the Compute Instance Admin (v1) role

explanation.summary: The account at cloudservices.gserviceaccount.com is the Google APIs Service Agent. It runs internal processes for Compute Engine, and a managed instance group creates and deletes its VMs through it.

option_breakdown.A: The account on the template is the identity the applications use; it is not the identity that creates the group's VMs.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The Google APIs Service Agent needs its Instance Group Manager Service Agent role to act for the group.
option_breakdown.C: A new group would rely on the same service agent, which would still lack its role.
option_breakdown.D: The VMs' own account does not create instances for the group, so more rights for it change nothing.

questions.title: Roles for the service account behind the Ops Agent
questions.summary: A VM's service account needs Logs Writer and Monitoring Metric Writer for the Ops Agent to send logs and metrics, and nothing broader.
questions.question: Linton Freight installs the Ops Agent on its VMs, which run as the dedicated service account fleet-vm. That account has no roles yet. The agent must be able to send the VMs' logs to Cloud Logging and their metrics to Cloud Monitoring, and the account should receive no other access. Which two roles should be granted to fleet-vm on the project? (Choose two.)

options.A: Logs Viewer
options.B: Monitoring Viewer
options.C: Logs Writer
options.D: Monitoring Metric Writer

explanation.summary: The Ops Agent authenticates as the VM's service account. Writing log entries needs Logs Writer and writing metric data needs Monitoring Metric Writer; reading either is not required.

option_breakdown.A: Logs Viewer reads log entries; the agent has to write them.
option_breakdown.B: Monitoring Viewer reads metrics and dashboards; the agent has to write metric data.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Logs Writer lets the agent send the VMs' log entries to Cloud Logging.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Monitoring Metric Writer lets the agent send the VMs' metrics to Cloud Monitoring.
option_breakdown.E: Editor would let the agent write both, but it also grants change rights on nearly everything in the project.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member="serviceAccount:fleet-vm@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com" --role="roles/logging.logWriter"
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member="serviceAccount:fleet-vm@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com" --role="roles/monitoring.metricWriter"

questions.title: The role an app needs to reach Cloud SQL through the proxy
questions.summary: A service account that connects through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy needs Cloud SQL Client, which carries the connect permission and no administrative rights.
questions.question: An order service at Ravenglass Books runs on a Compute Engine VM as the service account orders-app and connects to a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in the same project through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy. The proxy fails to connect because orders-app has no Cloud SQL role. The service only opens connections and runs SQL with its database user; it must not change or view the instance's configuration. Which role should orders-app be granted?

options.A: Cloud SQL Admin
options.B: Cloud SQL Viewer
options.C: Cloud SQL Client
options.D: Cloud SQL Editor

explanation.summary: The Auth Proxy authorizes a connection with the caller's IAM identity. Cloud SQL Client contains the cloudsql.instances.connect permission, which is what connecting needs.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud SQL Admin can connect, but it can also create, change and delete instances, far more than an application should hold.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud SQL Viewer can read the configuration of instances, which is not wanted, and it cannot open a connection.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud SQL Client authorizes a principal to connect to Cloud SQL instances and nothing administrative.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud SQL Editor can connect and can also manage existing instances, which the service must not do.

questions.title: Signed URLs from a service with no key file
questions.summary: Without a key file, signing a Cloud Storage URL uses signBlob, which the service account gets from Token Creator on itself.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service at Ribblesdale Media runs as the service account media-api and must hand out signed URLs so that customers can download single objects from a private bucket for ten minutes. The service has no key file, by policy. Reading the objects works, but creating a signed URL fails with an error naming the permission iam.serviceAccounts.signBlob. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Create a key for media-api and mount the key file into the service
options.B: Grant media-api the Service Account Token Creator role on itself
options.C: Grant media-api the Storage Admin role on the private bucket
options.D: Make the objects public and stop using signed URLs

explanation.summary: A signed URL carries a signature made with the service account's private key. With no key file, the signature comes from the signBlob method, whose permission is part of Service Account Token Creator.

option_breakdown.A: A key file would allow signing locally, but policy forbids keys and the Google-managed key can sign instead.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Token Creator on the account includes signBlob, which signs payloads such as Cloud Storage signed URLs.
option_breakdown.C: The error is about signing, not about access to objects; a broader storage role does not add signBlob.
option_breakdown.D: Public objects are readable by anyone for ever, not by one customer for ten minutes.

questions.title: Terraform from laptops, applied as a service account
questions.summary: Terraform run locally acts as a service account when the engineer holds Token Creator on it and a local ADC file is created with impersonation.
questions.question: Engineers at Hebden Systems run terraform apply from their laptops. All changes must be made as the service account tf-deployer, which holds the deployment roles; the engineers themselves hold no roles on the projects. Creating service account keys is blocked by policy. Which two things are needed so that Terraform on a laptop acts as tf-deployer? (Choose two.)

options.A: Service Account Token Creator for the engineers on tf-deployer
options.B: A key for tf-deployer referenced by GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
options.C: The Editor role for the engineers on every target project
options.D: A local ADC file created with impersonation of tf-deployer
options.E: Service Account User for the engineers on tf-deployer

explanation.summary: Terraform uses Application Default Credentials. A local ADC file set up with impersonation makes it act as the service account, and creating those credentials requires Token Creator on the account.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Impersonating tf-deployer requires the Token Creator role on that service account.
option_breakdown.B: This depends on a service account key, which policy blocks.
option_breakdown.C: With Editor the engineers would act as themselves with broad rights, not as tf-deployer.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Terraform automatically uses a local ADC file that was set up with service account impersonation.
option_breakdown.E: Service Account User allows attaching the account to resources, not obtaining credentials for it on a laptop.

questions.title: QUOTA_EXCEEDED when Pods ask for tokens
questions.summary: Token exchanges for Workload Identity Federation for GKE count against a Security Token Service quota that can be raised.
questions.question: A GKE cluster at Garsdale Media runs several thousand short-lived Pods per minute, each of which requests Google Cloud credentials through Workload Identity Federation for GKE. At peak, many Pods fail to authenticate and their logs show QUOTA_EXCEEDED errors from the token exchange. The workloads cannot be made to start less often. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Request a higher Token exchange requests per minute quota
options.B: Request a higher regional CPUS quota for the node pools
options.C: Give every Pod a service account key to avoid the exchange
options.D: Enable the feature a second time on each node pool

explanation.summary: The GKE metadata server exchanges each Kubernetes token at Security Token Service, whose Exchange Token API has a per-minute quota. Like other quotas, it can be raised from the Quotas & System Limits page.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The error comes from the token exchange quota, and an increase can be requested for it.
option_breakdown.B: The Pods are running; it is their token requests that are refused, so compute quota is not the limit.
option_breakdown.C: Keys would bypass the exchange by reintroducing long-lived secrets into thousands of Pods.
option_breakdown.D: The feature is either on or off for a node pool; enabling it again adds no capacity.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > IAM & Admin > Quotas & System Limits > filter: Token exchange requests per minute > Edit

questions.title: The person who looks after images and snapshots
questions.summary: Compute Storage Admin manages disks, images and snapshots without rights over VM instances.
questions.question: At Reeth Engineering one technician maintains the golden images and the disk snapshots of the project re-plant: creating, updating and deleting disks, images and snapshots. The technician must not be able to create, change or delete VM instances, and should not hold a basic role. Which predefined role should the technician be granted on the project?

options.A: Compute Storage Admin
options.B: Compute Instance Admin (v1)
options.C: Compute Viewer
options.D: Storage Admin

explanation.summary: Compute Engine has a predefined role for exactly the storage side of the service: disks, images and snapshots. It is meant for someone who manages images without the Editor role.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Compute Storage Admin can create, modify and delete disks, images and snapshots, and no instances.
option_breakdown.B: Instance Admin can create, change and delete VM instances, which the technician must not do.
option_breakdown.C: Compute Viewer can only read Compute Engine resources; it cannot create an image or a snapshot.
option_breakdown.D: Storage Admin is the Cloud Storage role for buckets and objects, not for Compute Engine disks or images.

questions.title: Any Terraform Cloud organization could get in
questions.summary: Multi-tenant identity providers use one issuer for all tenants, so the provider needs an attribute condition that accepts only the trusted organization.
questions.question: Selside Systems lets its Terraform Cloud workspaces deploy to Google Cloud through Workload Identity Federation. A reviewer notices that the workload identity provider only checks the issuer URL of the tokens, and that Terraform Cloud uses the same issuer URL for every customer's organization. What should be added so that only tokens from Selside's own Terraform Cloud organization are accepted?

options.A: A second provider in the pool for the same issuer URL
options.B: A longer token lifetime in the provider's settings
options.C: A firewall rule that allows only Terraform Cloud's IP ranges
options.D: An attribute condition on the provider that checks the organization

explanation.summary: Federation trusts a token by its issuer. With a multi-tenant provider the issuer identifies the whole service, so an attribute condition must check a claim that identifies the trusted tenant.

option_breakdown.A: A second provider for the same issuer trusts the same tokens again and adds ambiguity.
option_breakdown.B: Token lifetime has no bearing on which organization's tokens are accepted.
option_breakdown.C: The token exchange is an authentication step; other customers of the service come from the same addresses.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The attribute condition makes the provider accept only tokens issued for the trusted organization.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers update-oidc tfc --workload-identity-pool=POOL_ID --location=global --attribute-condition='assertion.terraform_organization_name=="selside"'
